He has remained one of ambient music's most prolific and least commercially visible figures, sustained by a devoted audience built almost entirely outside the mainstream music industry.

classicAlbums.title: Structures from Silence
classicAlbums.classicReason: Structures from Silence unfolds across three side-long pieces of synthesizer tone, each one built from the same patient method: a single harmonic idea, allowed to breathe and shift almost imperceptibly over twenty minutes at a time. The title track drifts forward so gradually that individual moments barely register as change, yet the piece arrives somewhere completely different from where it began. Nothing here reaches for a melody in any conventional sense, trusting texture and duration instead. It remains the album most credited with giving American ambient music its own voice, independent of the European synthesizer tradition it grew out of.

artists.previewAlbum: Structures From Silence (30th Anniversary Deluxe Remastered Edition)

artists.name: Sneaker Pimps
artists.bio:
Sneaker Pimps formed in Southampton, England in 1994 around producers Liam Howe and Chris Corner, later adding singer Kelli Ali, and arrived directly in the wake of Massive Attack and Portishead's early-1990s Bristol trip-hop breakthrough. The band's sound leaned into the same hip-hop-derived beats and cinematic atmosphere, though with a colder, more electronic edge than either of their acknowledged touchstones.

Becoming X, their 1996 debut, became a UK chart success on the strength of "6 Underground," a song reworked into a more radio-friendly single mix after the album's initial release. Ali left the band shortly afterward, with Corner taking over lead vocals for the records that followed, before the group eventually dissolved and its members moved into other projects, most notably Corner's later work as IAMX. Sneaker Pimps remain most closely associated with a single commercial peak rather than a long career arc, but that peak captured trip-hop's crossover moment about as precisely as any other record from the period.

classicAlbums.title: Becoming X
classicAlbums.classicReason: Becoming X pairs Kelli Ali's cool, detached vocal with Liam Howe and Chris Corner's dense, cinematic production, closer in spirit to Massive Attack's paranoid sprawl than Portishead's torch-song intimacy. "6 Underground" is the clearest distillation of that sound, its stalking bassline and looping guitar sample carrying the album's biggest hook without ever losing the record's overall chill. The rest of the album stays in a similarly nocturnal register, favoring mood over obvious singles. It remains the release most responsible for carrying Bristol-style trip-hop production into mainstream UK chart success.

artists.name: Slayyyter
artists.bio:
Slayyyter began releasing hyperpop-adjacent bedroom-pop singles online in the late 2010s, building an audience through mixtapes before pursuit of a fuller pop sound took hold across a string of increasingly polished releases. Her music leans on hooks pulled from turn-of-the-millennium chart pop, filtered through a deliberately maximalist, internet-native production style.

Her self-titled debut mixtape arrived in 2019, followed by Troubled Paradise in 2021, each record pushing her sound a little further toward glossier, more conventional pop production. Worst Girl in America, her third album, arrived in 2026, and she has described it as a deliberate return to the sound of her own teenage years after those more polished releases. It became her highest-charting release to date, arriving after years of steadily building an audience through independent releases rather than a single breakout moment. Slayyyter's catalog has continued to track a fairly direct line between bedroom-pop experimentation and pop stardom, without ever fully arriving at either extreme.

classicAlbums.title: Worst Girl in America
classicAlbums.classicReason: Worst Girl in America leans back into the sound of Slayyyter's own adolescence, trading some of her most recent records' polish for something rawer and more personal. "Beat Up Chanels" carries that shift clearly, its hook built from the same turn-of-the-millennium pop instincts that first drew her to music, delivered with more bite than nostalgia. She has described the record as a last-ditch effort at making something she could be genuinely proud of, and that stakes-raising shows in the writing throughout. It became her highest-charting release, suggesting the more personal approach paid off commercially as well as artistically.

artists.name: Kero Kero Bonito
artists.bio:
Kero Kero Bonito formed in London in 2011 around producers Gus Lobban and Jamie Bulled, later joined by vocalist Sarah Midori Perry after they found her through an online talent search, blending playful, hyper-melodic electronic pop sung partly in Japanese and partly in English. Their early mixtapes and singles leaned toward bright, video-game-indebted production, building a devoted online following well before the band toured widely or signed to a proper label.

Time 'n' Place, their second album, arrived in 2018 and marked a deliberate turn toward live guitars and a more anxious, less immediately cheerful atmosphere than the music that had built their audience. The band continued expanding their sound on subsequent releases, moving between that guitar-driven direction and a return to denser electronic production depending on the record. Kero Kero Bonito's catalog now reads as a study in refusing to stay put in any single genre, treating each album as license to start over.

classicAlbums.title: Time 'n' Place
classicAlbums.classicReason: Time 'n' Place trades Kero Kero Bonito's earlier bright, hyper-melodic electronic pop for live guitars and a genuinely anxious undertone, the sound of a band deliberately unsettling its own audience. "Make Believe" carries that tension clearly, its jittery guitar and Sarah Midori Perry's still-bright vocal sitting uneasily against lyrics considerably darker than the band's earlier work suggested. The record's suburban unease drew on a specific, deliberately un-glamorous well of British and American guitar music rather than any electronic lineage. It stands as the album that proved the band's earlier cheerfulness was a choice rather than a limitation.

artists.name: death's dynamic shroud
artists.bio:
death's dynamic shroud formed in the United States in the early 2010s, built around a shifting lineup that has centered on Tech Honors and James Webster, working within vaporwave's slowed-down, sample-heavy palette while pushing it toward something closer to genuine pop songwriting. The band draws on 1990s Western alternative rock and Japanese and Korean pop and film samples in roughly equal measure, a combination that sets them apart from vaporwave's more purely ambient or elevator-music-indebted wing.

I'll Try Living Like This, released in 2015, originally appeared under the fuller name death's dynamic shroud.wmv, a suffix later dropped as the band's music moved further from vaporwave's internet-native, meme-adjacent origins. The band has continued releasing music steadily since, refining the same blend of hazy nostalgia and genuine songcraft across further albums. Their catalog has aged into one of the more melodically ambitious corners of a genre often defined by its anonymity.

classicAlbums.title: I'll Try Living Like This
classicAlbums.classicReason: I'll Try Living Like This pulls vaporwave's slowed-down samples and hazy nostalgia toward something closer to actual songwriting, treating the genre's usual tools as a palette rather than the whole point. "내 마음은 떨고" folds a mournful, half-buried vocal into warped, K-pop-adjacent samples, turning source material usually played for genre-signifying irony into something genuinely melancholic. The album favors emotional clarity over vaporwave's more common ironic distance throughout. It remains one of the records most credited with proving the genre could sustain real songwriting rather than just atmosphere.

artists.bio:
2814 formed as a collaboration between the French producer HKE and Hong Kong-based artist t e l e p a t h, working within vaporwave's ambient, city-pop-sampling wing rather than the genre's more overtly ironic strand. Their music builds long, drifting tracks from processed synthesizer pads and half-recognizable samples of 1980s Japanese pop and corporate soundtrack music, aiming for genuine atmosphere rather than any winking commentary on consumer culture.

Birth of a New Day, released in 2015 on the Dream Catalogue label, became the project's best-known release, its two contributors working largely apart from each other before combining their halves of each track. The duo continued releasing music only sporadically afterward, maintaining the same anonymous, low-profile presence that has defined vaporwave's more serious wing throughout its existence. 2814's catalog remains a reference point within the genre precisely because it treated vaporwave's tools as capable of real, unironic beauty.

classicAlbums.title: Birth of a New Day
classicAlbums.classicReason: Birth of a New Day stretches synthesizer pads and half-buried samples into long, drifting tracks that favor genuine atmosphere over vaporwave's more common ironic distance. "恍惚" builds slowly from a simple repeating pad into something closer to genuine ambient music, its samples treated and layered until their original source becomes almost unrecognizable. The album's two contributors worked largely apart from one another, yet the record holds together as a single, coherent mood throughout. It remains one of vaporwave's most widely cited records specifically because it plays its beauty completely straight.

artists.name: George Clanton
artists.bio:
George Clanton began releasing music in the early 2010s within the vaporwave scene before pushing his own sound toward a warmer, more song-based synth-pop, eventually founding the label 100% Electronica to release his own records and those of like-minded artists. His music pulls together the atmosphere of 1980s and '90s synthesizer pop with a distinctly present-day sense of nostalgia for those decades' textures rather than a straightforward revival of them.

Slide, his second album, arrived in 2018 and became the record that carried him furthest beyond vaporwave's internet-native subculture into a wider synth-pop audience. Clanton has continued releasing music and running his label steadily since, also touring behind his records more extensively than most artists to emerge from the same scene. His catalog has increasingly positioned him as a bridge between vaporwave's originating community and a broader synth-pop audience that arrived without knowing that history.

classicAlbums.title: Slide
classicAlbums.classicReason: Slide wraps warm, chorus-drenched synthesizers and driving drum-machine rhythms around genuinely direct pop songwriting, closer to a lost 1980s radio hit than to vaporwave's more ironic or ambient tendencies. "Make It Forever" carries that directness at its clearest, its shimmering hook riding a steady pulse that never lets the song's nostalgia curdle into pure pastiche. The production stays lush throughout without ever feeling like an exercise in genre imitation. It remains the album most responsible for carrying Clanton's version of vaporwave's warmth to an audience well beyond that scene's original internet home.

artists.name: FKA twigs
artists.bio:
FKA twigs, born Tahliah Barnett, began releasing music from London in the early 2010s, having worked previously as a backup dancer, and built a sound around hushed, technically intricate vocals set against skeletal, texturally adventurous production. Her early EPs drew immediate comparisons to Björk and other art-pop antecedents, though her own stated influences run more toward R&B and dance music than any single lineage.

LP1, her debut album, arrived in 2014 to widespread critical acclaim and a Mercury Prize shortlisting, establishing her as one of the decade's most distinctive new voices in art-pop. She has continued releasing music and pursuing acting work in the years since, expanding her sound across further albums while keeping the same commitment to meticulous, unhurried production. FKA twigs has remained one of the clearest reference points for a generation of art-pop and R&B-adjacent artists who followed her.

classicAlbums.title: LP1
classicAlbums.classicReason: LP1 sets FKA twigs's hushed, technically demanding vocal runs against production so skeletal it sometimes threatens to disappear entirely, leaving enormous space for her voice to fill. "Two Weeks" is the album's clearest statement, its minimal, off-kilter beat carrying a vocal performance that moves between vulnerability and outright command within the same verse, the lyric itself turning patience into a kind of threat. The whole record favors negative space over density, trusting silence as much as sound. It remains the release most responsible for establishing her as one of art-pop's most technically distinctive voices.

artists.name: Sheena Ringo
artists.bio:
Sheena Ringo emerged in Japan in the late 1990s, quickly establishing herself as one of J-pop's most distinctive and uncompromising voices, pulling together rock, jazz, enka and classical arrangement into a sound built around her own theatrical, technically demanding vocal performances. She wrote and produced her own material from the start, unusual for a young woman working within a major-label pop system at the time.

Shōso Strip, her second album, arrived in 2000 and pushed her sound further into orchestral, big-band-inflected territory than her debut had. She went on to found the collective Tokyo Jihen later in the decade, splitting her subsequent output between that project and a long-running solo career, and has remained a major and often boundary-pushing presence in Japanese popular music for over two decades since. Her catalog outside Japan remains under-documented in English relative to her actual stature at home.

classicAlbums.title: Shōso Strip
classicAlbums.classicReason: Shōso Strip pushes Sheena Ringo's sound toward big-band and orchestral arrangement, giving her theatrical, technically demanding voice a genuinely cinematic frame to work against. "本能 (Honnō)" carries that ambition clearly, brass and strings swelling behind a vocal performance that swings between restraint and full-throated drama within a single verse. The album never settles into a single genre, moving between rock, jazz and orchestral pop with total confidence in each. It stands as one of the records most responsible for establishing her reputation as one of Japanese pop's most technically fearless performers.

artists.name: Grimes
artists.bio:
Grimes, born Claire Boucher, began recording lo-fi electronic music in Montreal in the late 2000s, self-releasing early albums like Geidi Primes and Halfaxa largely alone with cheap software before developing a more layered, dream-pop-inflected sound built around looped vocals and synthesizer textures. She has pushed back on frequent critical comparisons to Björk as reductive, even while acknowledging real admiration for her, preferring to describe her own music on its own terms.

Visions, her third album, arrived in 2012 and became her commercial and critical breakthrough, recorded largely during a self-imposed period of isolation fueled by amphetamines and near-total sleep deprivation. She continued expanding her sound across further albums afterward, moving toward denser, more maximalist production and increasingly high-profile collaborations. Grimes's catalog has tracked an unusually steep arc from underground bedroom-pop experimentation to mainstream visibility within the space of a single decade.

classicAlbums.title: Visions
classicAlbums.classicReason: Visions layers looped vocals, cheap synthesizers and dense reverb into something that sounds simultaneously homemade and genuinely otherworldly, the product of an intensely isolated recording process. "Oblivion" is the clearest distillation of that method, its deadpan vocal delivery riding a driving, almost martial beat that turns a lyric about vulnerability into something that sounds strangely triumphant. The whole album favors texture and repetition over conventional song structure without ever losing its pop instincts. It remains the release most responsible for establishing Grimes as one of the decade's defining bedroom-electronic voices.

artists.name: Magdalena Bay
artists.bio:
Magdalena Bay formed around Mica Tenenbaum and Matthew Lewin, who met as teenagers and began releasing music together after relocating to Los Angeles, building a sound that pairs Tenenbaum's melodic songwriting with Lewin's dense, maximalist synth-pop production. Their early releases established a strong visual and conceptual identity alongside the music, drawing on both nostalgic synth textures and contemporary digital aesthetics in equal measure.

Imaginal Disk, their second album, arrived in 2024 built around a loose narrative concept about identity and transformation, pushing their sound toward more orchestral and cinematic territory than their earlier, more straightforwardly poppy work. The duo has continued developing that same combination of conceptual ambition and pop songcraft since, building a devoted following through both their recorded output and elaborate live visuals. Magdalena Bay's catalog has moved steadily from internet-native synth-pop toward something more ambitious in both sound and scope.

classicAlbums.title: Imaginal Disk
classicAlbums.classicReason: Imaginal Disk wraps a loose concept about identity and metamorphosis around Magdalena Bay's densest, most orchestrated production yet, swapping some of their earlier work's straightforward pop hooks for something stranger and more cinematic. "Death & Romance" carries that ambition clearly, horns and layered vocal harmonies building toward a climax that feels genuinely theatrical rather than merely maximalist. The album commits fully to its narrative conceit without ever losing sight of Mica Tenenbaum's melodic instincts underneath. It stands as the record where the duo's conceptual ambitions and their pop songwriting finally matched each other in scale.

artists.name: Xiu Xiu
artists.bio:
Xiu Xiu formed around Jamie Stewart in San Jose, California in 2002, building a catalog defined by unflinching, often disturbing lyrical content set against a constantly shifting instrumental palette that has moved between skeletal acoustic arrangements, harsh electronics and orchestral drama from one album to the next. Stewart has remained the band's sole constant across dozens of collaborators, giving unusually candid interviews about the personal material behind the songs.

Fabulous Muscles, their third album, arrived in 2004 and became the record most widely credited with establishing the band's reputation, pairing that confrontational songwriting with some of their most accessible arrangements to date. The band has continued releasing music at a rapid pace in the two decades since, moving through dramatically different sonic phases while keeping the same commitment to lyrical directness. Xiu Xiu's influence has surfaced widely among later artists working in confessional and experimental pop alike, even where the band's own commercial profile has stayed modest.

classicAlbums.title: Fabulous Muscles
classicAlbums.classicReason: Fabulous Muscles pairs Jamie Stewart's most unflinching lyrics yet with arrangements that swing between skeletal electronics and sudden orchestral swells, never settling into a single texture for long. "I Luv the Valley OH!" carries that contrast at its most extreme, a tender, almost childlike melody set against lyrics that confront trauma and desire with total directness. The production throughout stays raw enough that nothing feels aestheticized or safely distanced from its subject matter. It remains the album most responsible for establishing Xiu Xiu's reputation as one of experimental pop's most confrontational and influential voices.

artists.name: Mid-Air Thief
artists.bio:
Mid-Air Thief is the recording name of Kenny Suh, a Korean-American musician who began releasing dense, collage-like psychedelic pop from relative obscurity before slowly building an online following through word of mouth. His music layers acoustic guitar, sampled sound and electronic production into something that resists easy placement within either American indie or Korean pop traditions, drawing on both without settling into either.

Crumbling, his debut album, arrived in 2018 after Suh spent years assembling it largely alone, and its detailed, headphone-rewarding production gradually found an audience well beyond what its quiet initial release suggested. He has given very few interviews since, keeping most of his creative process private even as the record's reputation grew. Mid-Air Thief's small catalog remains under-documented relative to its actual influence, a gap that owes as much to the artist's own reticence as to any lack of interest from listeners.

classicAlbums.title: Crumbling
classicAlbums.classicReason: Crumbling layers acoustic guitar, field recordings and warped electronic production into a dense, headphone-rewarding collage that rewards repeated listening more than any single pass. "These Chains" folds a genuinely pretty vocal melody into a constantly shifting bed of samples and texture, never settling long enough to feel predictable. The whole album favors accumulation over hooks, treating each song as a small, detailed world rather than a single statement. It remains the release most responsible for building Mid-Air Thief's reputation as one of psychedelic pop's most quietly ambitious voices.

artists.name: Candy Claws
artists.bio:
Candy Claws formed around Fort Collins, Colorado in the mid-2000s under the direction of Ryan Hoover, building a hazy, richly layered take on shoegaze and dream-pop steeped in the sound of My Bloody Valentine and, by Hoover's own account, the more obscure Starflyer 59. The band's records lean heavily on dense guitar textures and reverb-soaked production, favoring atmosphere and repetition over conventional song structure.

Ceres & Calypso in the Deep Time, their third album, arrived in 2013, built loosely around themes of deep geological time and the natural world. The band has released only sporadically since, sustained by a small but devoted following built almost entirely through word of mouth rather than wider commercial attention. Candy Claws' catalog remains a minor but genuinely distinctive entry within American shoegaze, more cited by fellow musicians than widely known outside the genre's smaller circles.

classicAlbums.title: Ceres & Calypso in the Deep Time
classicAlbums.classicReason: Ceres & Calypso in the Deep Time wraps dense, reverb-soaked guitar textures around a loose concept about geological time and the natural world, favoring immersive atmosphere over conventional songwriting. "Pangaea Girls" carries that mood clearly, its washed-out guitars and half-buried vocal drifting along without ever resolving into a sharp hook, more interested in accumulation than statement. The whole record rewards long, uninterrupted listening more than individual tracks pulled out on their own. It stands as the clearest distillation of a band more interested in mood and scale than in radio-ready songwriting.

artists.previewAlbum: Ceres & Calypso in the Deep Time (10th Anniversary)

artists.name: The Marías
artists.bio:
The Marías formed in Los Angeles in 2016 around María Zardoya and Josh Conway, building a sound that draws far more heavily on R&B, soul and Latin pop than on the indie-electronic tradition they sit adjacent to, with Zardoya moving fluidly between English and Spanish across the band's catalog. Their sound leans on hazy, reverb-heavy production and Zardoya's smoky, unhurried vocal delivery, closer in spirit to classic soul and bossa nova than to any strictly electronic lineage.

Submarine, their second full-length album, arrived in 2024, expanding the band's sound to a fuller, more expansive scale than their earlier, more intimate releases. The band has continued touring and recording steadily since, building a large and rapidly growing audience largely through streaming rather than any single crossover moment. The Marías now sit at the edge of several different scenes at once, claimed by dream-pop, R&B and Latin pop audiences without belonging fully to any one of them.

classicAlbums.title: Submarine
classicAlbums.classicReason: Submarine wraps María Zardoya's smoky, unhurried vocal in lush, reverb-heavy production that owes as much to classic soul and bossa nova as to any dream-pop lineage. "No One Noticed" carries that blend at its most immediate, a warm, mid-tempo groove giving Zardoya's voice room to stretch without ever rushing the song's languid pace. The album stays committed to that same hazy, unhurried mood throughout, rarely raising its voice even at its most emotionally direct. It stands as the record that carried the band's sound to its widest audience yet without sanding down what made it distinctive.

artists.name: Alex G
artists.bio:
Alex Giannascoli began releasing music as Alex G from a childhood bedroom outside Philadelphia, uploading a steady run of lo-fi folk, pop, and warped country songs to Bandcamp through his teens and early twenties with no label involved. His hushed, often pitch-shifted vocal delivery grew partly out of necessity — he has cited Elliott Smith's own whispery singing directly, explaining that it made staying in tune easier and, as a practical bonus, let him record without waking his roommates.

That homemade catalog eventually found a wider audience, and after years of self-releasing directly to Bandcamp, Giannascoli signed a record deal; he now records for RCA, though the guitar-forward, detail-heavy songwriting hasn't been smoothed out by the move. House of Sugar, released in 2019, arrived well into that shift from bedroom experimentation toward denser, more unsettling arrangements. He has also been known to play Ween over the venue PA before his own shows, a habit that says as much about his sensibility as any interview.

classicAlbums.title: House of Sugar
classicAlbums.classicReason: House of Sugar folds Alex G's bedroom-pop instincts into denser, stranger arrangements, pitch-shifted vocals and queasy, off-kilter twang sitting alongside genuinely pretty melodies. "Gretel" pairs a plainspoken, almost folk-song structure with production that keeps tilting the ground underneath it, never settling into a single genre. The record trusts unease and prettiness to coexist in the same verse without resolving the tension. It remains the clearest document of Giannascoli's move from raw home recordings toward something more meticulously constructed without losing the strangeness that made the early tapes compelling.

artists.name: MJ Lenderman
artists.bio:
MJ Lenderman is based in Asheville, North Carolina, where he also plays guitar in the band Wednesday alongside his own solo career, moving between the two projects' overlapping but distinct songwriting sensibilities. His own work draws on a specifically American lineage of wry, plainspoken songwriting, citing Jason Molina, Silver Jews, Neil Young, and Drive-By Truckers as reference points for combining dry humor with genuine ache.

Manning Fireworks, released in 2024, became the album that carried Lenderman's songwriting furthest beyond Wednesday's orbit and into wider recognition on its own terms. His rise has coincided with a broader resurgence of interest in the kind of unfussy, character-driven indie rock and alt-country songwriting he draws from, positioning him as a connective figure between older underground traditions and a newer audience discovering them through his records, largely by accident rather than any deliberate campaign.

classicAlbums.title: Manning Fireworks
classicAlbums.classicReason: Manning Fireworks pairs MJ Lenderman's dry, deadpan sense of humor with genuinely aching guitar-driven songwriting, never letting one undercut the other. "She's Leaving You" turns a specific, almost embarrassingly detailed scene into something both funny and quietly devastating, Lenderman's unhurried vocal delivery selling the joke and the heartbreak in the same breath. The arrangements stay loose and unpolished without ever sounding unfinished, guitars left ragged rather than sanded down for the studio. It's the record that established him as a distinct songwriting voice rather than simply Wednesday's guitarist.

artists.name: Wednesday
artists.bio:
Karly Hartzman leads Wednesday out of Asheville, North Carolina, having gotten her first musical experience singing in a synagogue choir before eventually building a sound she has described simply as an attempt "to make shoegaze with lyrics that are worth listening to." She has cited memoirist Mary Karr as a lyrical influence, and after hearing Drive-By Truckers' "Let There Be Rock," wrote "Chosen to Deserve" using her own memories to fill the same premise of describing a difficult childhood.

Rat Saw God, released in 2023, became the album that brought Wednesday its widest attention yet, arriving after several years of steady work sharpening the band's sound. MJ Lenderman, who also records solo, plays guitar in the band, one of several overlapping connections running through Asheville's small but increasingly visible songwriting scene, whose rising profile Wednesday has helped bring wider attention to.

classicAlbums.title: Rat Saw God
classicAlbums.classicReason: Rat Saw God pairs Wednesday's thick, distorted shoegaze guitar wall with Karly Hartzman's plainspoken, almost novelistic Southern storytelling. "Bull Believer" spends most of its long runtime as a slow, patiently building tension before erupting into a screamed, cathartic finale that earns its length by refusing to rush toward it. The lyrics favor sharp, specific detail over vague sentiment throughout, giving the noise something concrete and lived-in to hang onto. It remains the album that fully merged the band's atmospheric, shoegaze-indebted instincts with Hartzman's increasingly literary songwriting.

artists.name: Bonnie Prince Billy
artists.bio:
Will Oldham had already recorded for most of the 1990s as Palace Brothers and Palace Music before adopting the name Bonnie Prince Billy, a shift that let him keep reinventing his catalog's identity without abandoning its stark, plainspoken core. His songs favor spare acoustic arrangements and a stark, often harrowing personal candor, delivered in a frail, unadorned voice that resists any hint of performance.

I See a Darkness, released in 1999, arrived as Oldham settled fully into the Bonnie Prince Billy name after years of shifting monikers. Younger songwriters in the confessional and freak-folk traditions, including Phil Elverum, have cited him directly as a reference point for treating plainness itself as a kind of intensity. Oldham has continued recording prolifically since, moving between traditional-leaning records and stranger experiments without ever settling into a fixed persona, releasing albums at a pace few of his peers have matched.

classicAlbums.title: I See a Darkness
classicAlbums.classicReason: I See a Darkness strips songwriting down to voice, acoustic guitar, and unflinching subject matter, mortality and dread delivered without a trace of melodrama. The title track sits at its center, a plainspoken meditation on depression and death delivered in a voice too frail and unguarded to read as performance. That refusal to dress up the bleakness is what gives the record its power — nothing here asks to be admired, only heard. It remains the album most responsible for establishing Oldham as a foundational voice in confessional and freak-folk songwriting alike.

artists.name: Turnstile
artists.bio:
Turnstile formed in Baltimore in 2010, emerging from a hardcore lineage that runs directly back through Bad Brains and Minor Threat even as the band pushed steadily outward from that tradition's usual boundaries. Early releases stuck closer to the tradition's conventional attack, but the band's sound kept absorbing outside elements with each successive release, without ever fully cutting ties to the scene it came up in.

Glow On, released in 2021, completed that transformation into something that drew in listeners well outside hardcore's usual audience while never fully abandoning the genre's intensity. The record's genre-blurring success became part of its own story, sparking ongoing debate within the scene about whether Turnstile still belonged to hardcore at all or had simply outgrown the label entirely, a question the band itself has never seemed especially interested in resolving one way or the other.

classicAlbums.title: Glow On
classicAlbums.classicReason: Glow On fuses hardcore's speed and aggression with melody, groove, and a spacious, almost pop-adjacent production that few bands in the genre had attempted. "Blackout" pairs a chugging, hardcore-rooted riff with a soaring, genuinely catchy chorus, refusing to treat heaviness and hookiness as incompatible. The record moves fluidly between blast-beat intensity and moments of near-danceable groove without the shifts ever feeling forced or gimmicky. It remains the album most responsible for pulling Turnstile, and hardcore more broadly, toward a much wider and more varied audience.

artists.name: Ariel Pink
artists.bio:
Ariel Pink began recording alone on an eight-track Portastudio as a teenager, accumulating well over 200 cassettes of warped, degraded pop between 1996 and 2003 before any of it was formally released. He has cited the sound of The Cure's Faith as a formative discovery, saying it "typified everything I wanted to be, which is mediocrity, ambiguity, totally serious and totally helpless" — a description that doubles as a fair account of his own aesthetic.

Before Today, released in 2010, marked his move from cassette-only obscurity into a full studio setting and a wider audience. Pink has since been widely credited as a godfather of hypnagogic pop and chillwave, genres built directly on the woozy, half-remembered pop sound he spent years perfecting alone. That influence has persisted even as his own career has remained defiantly hard to categorize, veering between genuine pop craft and deliberate provocation in roughly equal measure.

classicAlbums.title: Before Today
classicAlbums.classicReason: Before Today translates a decade of degraded cassette experiments into full-band arrangements without losing their foggy, tape-warped disorientation. "Round and Round" shifts through several distinct sections — a proggy detour, a yacht-rock chorus — that shouldn't cohere but do, anchored by a hook that sounds beamed in from another decade entirely. The production keeps everything slightly warped, as though the tape were degrading in real time, filtering even the catchiest moments through a nostalgia for pop music that never quite existed. It's the record most responsible for making Pink's hypnagogic haze legible as pop rather than pure novelty, without sanding down the strangeness that got him there.

artists.name: Perfume Genius
artists.bio:
Mike Hadreas began recording as Perfume Genius from his mother's home in Washington after moving back following a period of addiction and instability, building early songs around minimal piano and unflinchingly personal lyrics about trauma, sexuality, and recovery. He has cited Xiu Xiu directly, saying he loves how "intense and visceral and over the top" their songs can get, a quality that increasingly shaped his own music's willingness to push past conventional restraint.

No Shape, released in 2017, marked a significant turn in Hadreas's sound and brought him to his widest audience yet. Despite frequent critical comparisons to Talk Talk, Hadreas has said he had never actually heard the band before fans began making the connection, a case of critics hearing a lineage the artist arrived at independently. Perfume Genius has continued expanding that sound across subsequent releases and collaborations.

classicAlbums.title: No Shape
classicAlbums.classicReason: No Shape trades Perfume Genius's earlier minimalism for dense, maximalist production without losing the raw emotional directness underneath it. "Slip Away" builds from a hushed opening into a euphoric, string-laced climax, Mike Hadreas's voice moving from vulnerable to triumphant within a single song. The record treats joy and trauma as inseparable rather than opposing forces, letting both coexist in the same swelling arrangements without either one canceling the other out. It remains the album that pushed Hadreas's music from intimate confession toward something closer to full-blown, unguarded catharsis.

artists.name: Editors
artists.bio:
Editors formed in Birmingham in 2002, arriving as part of a mid-2000s wave of British bands that looked back past Britpop toward post-punk's colder, more cavernous end. The band has cited The Chameleons and Echo & the Bunnymen directly, and that lineage shows clearly across the group's early singles, a sound built as much for cavernous festival tents as for headphones.

The Back Room, released in 2005, introduced that sound to a wide UK audience and established Editors as one of the more commercially successful bands to emerge from the post-punk revival of the period. The band has continued recording and touring in the two decades since, refining and occasionally darkening its sound across several later albums while remaining closely identified with the atmosphere established on its debut, still filling the same large rooms its early singles were built for.

classicAlbums.title: The Back Room
classicAlbums.classicReason: The Back Room revives post-punk's coldest, most cavernous instincts and dresses them up as arena-ready anthems, reverb-drenched guitars circling Tom Smith's booming baritone. "Munich" pairs a tense, needling guitar riff with a chorus built to fill much larger rooms than the band was playing at the time, a tension that defines the whole record. Nothing here hides its debt to the Chameleons and Echo & the Bunnymen, yet the songwriting is confident enough not to feel like pure homage. It remains the clearest statement of the mid-2000s British post-punk revival's more anthemic wing.

artists.name: Mudhoney
artists.bio:
Mudhoney formed in Seattle in 1988, quickly becoming one of the foundational bands on the newly launched Sub Pop label and a key architect of the sound that would soon be marketed worldwide as grunge. The band has cited the Wipers directly as an influence, and their own fuzzed-out, garage-indebted guitar sound became a direct template for much of what followed out of the city; Kurt Cobain named Mudhoney his favorite band.

Superfuzz Bigmuff, released in 1988, was one of Sub Pop's very first releases and helped define the label's early identity. Mudhoney continued recording and touring for decades afterward, largely avoiding the mainstream breakthrough that reshaped the careers of several of their Seattle peers, and have remained closely associated with the noisiest, least polished end of the grunge sound they helped originate, outlasting many of the peers who overtook them commercially.

classicAlbums.title: Superfuzz Bigmuff
classicAlbums.classicReason: Superfuzz Bigmuff crams a handful of blown-out, feedback-soaked garage-punk songs into a short, exhilarating EP that helped define Sub Pop's earliest sound. It arrived the same year as the standalone single "Touch Me I'm Sick," whose fuzzed-out riff and gleefully sick lyrics became the song most identified with the band's early run even though it never appeared on the EP itself. Together they capture Mudhoney at its rawest, treating volume and distortion as ends in themselves rather than obstacles to a hook. Taken as a pair, the two releases remain the clearest document of grunge's underground, pre-fame moment.

artists.name: Tom Waits
artists.bio:
Tom Waits began his career in the early 1970s as a boozy lounge-jazz balladeer, a persona built on Beat-writer affectations and a graveled voice that only grew rougher over the following decade. Bob Dylan was an early and formative touchstone; Waits kept handwritten transcriptions of Dylan's lyrics on his bedroom wall, though his own influences ran at least as deep into blues, jazz, and Captain Beefheart's junkyard experimentalism as into any songwriter tradition.

Rain Dogs, released in 1985, arrived in the middle of Waits's decisive turn away from that early lounge persona toward the scrap-yard experimentalism he developed alongside his wife and collaborator Kathleen Brennan. The album consolidated a body of work built from found sounds, Beat-inflected storytelling, and an increasingly theatrical sense of composition, cementing Waits's reputation as one of American songwriting's most singular and least imitable figures, a reputation that has only grown since.

classicAlbums.title: Rain Dogs
classicAlbums.classicReason: Rain Dogs assembles clattering junkyard percussion, marimba, and Tom Waits's ruined-gravel voice into a sound that belongs to no other record before or since. "Time" pulls back from the album's noisier experiments into something closer to a devastated ballad, Waits's voice finding real tenderness underneath all the rasp. Elsewhere the record lurches between tango, blues, and something closer to carnival music without ever losing its own internal logic. It remains the clearest single document of Waits's transformation from lounge crooner into one of American music's most idiosyncratic storytellers.

artists.name: Songs: Ohia
artists.bio:
Jason Molina recorded as Songs: Ohia from 1996 to 2003, building a catalog of stark, reverb-heavy songs steeped in isolation, weather, and endurance, often recorded quickly and with a rotating cast of collaborators. He pushed back directly against frequent comparisons to Leonard Cohen, saying he hadn't actually heard a single Cohen song until he was nearly out of college, a lineage critics assumed rather than one he ever claimed himself.

Magnolia Electric Co., released in 2003, is both the final Songs: Ohia album and the first release credited to the renamed project, marking the exact transition point between the two, a rare instance of one record serving double duty. He continued recording as Magnolia Electric Co. for the rest of the decade before his death in 2013, a loss that only deepened the reputation of his catalog's stark honesty about hardship and mortality.

classicAlbums.title: Magnolia Electric Co.
classicAlbums.classicReason: Magnolia Electric Co. trades Songs: Ohia's stripped-down isolation for a fuller, classic-rock-indebted band sound without losing Jason Molina's stark, weather-beaten worldview. "Farewell Transmission" stretches past seven minutes on a repeated, mantra-like refrain, "the whole place is dark," that turns simple repetition into genuine dread. The record functions as both an ending and a beginning, closing out one project's name while opening the next. It remains the album most responsible for Molina's lasting reputation as one of the era's most unflinching songwriters about endurance and loss.

artists.name: Pinback
artists.bio:
Pinback formed in San Diego in 1998 around Rob Crow and Zach Smith, both veterans of the city's aggressive DIY scene through their earlier bands Heavy Vegetable and Three Mile Pilot respectively. The two brought sharply opposite relationships to influence into the same project: Smith has argued that fewer influences produce more original work, once claiming to own around twenty CDs total, while Crow is a voracious listener whose earlier band Heavy Vegetable name-checked Slint, Can, the Velvet Underground, Zappa, Captain Beefheart, the Residents, and Devo in a single song about what radio ignored.

Blue Screen Life, released in 2001, became the album where that tension between minimalism and dense reference points first resolved into a sound distinctly the band's own. Crow has also lent his voice to Drive Like Jehu's Yank Crime, and Pinback's debut album sampled drumming from the Minutemen's George Hurley, small details tracing the band's roots through San Diego's wider underground even as its own sound moved in a more melodic direction.

classicAlbums.title: Blue Screen Life
classicAlbums.classicReason: Blue Screen Life builds intricate, interlocking guitar and bass melodies into songs that feel meticulously constructed without ever sounding stiff. "Penelope" layers Rob Crow and Zach Smith's voices over an instrumental part that shifts and unspools gradually, rewarding close listening more than immediate hooks. The record's precision reflects the band's origins in San Diego's technically demanding underground scene, even as its melodic sensibility softens that scene's harder edges. It remains the clearest statement of Pinback's particular, hard-won blend of math-rock intricacy and genuine pop instinct.

artists.name: Waxahatchee
artists.bio:
Katie Crutchfield records as Waxahatchee, taking the name from Waxahatchee Creek near her childhood home in Alabama, after earlier fronting the punk-leaning band P.S. Eliot. She has cited Lucinda Williams as her single most direct songwriting influence, saying her own approach to structure is "identical to Lucinda" and noting that, like Williams, she rarely writes a bridge into her songs. Crutchfield has also recorded Jason Molina covers, on the Great Thunder EP, tracing another line back through American songwriting's plainspoken tradition.

Saint Cloud, released in 2020, arrived after a period of major personal change, including a newly sober outlook that reshaped Crutchfield's songwriting and life alike. The album became her most widely praised to date, read by many as the record where her literary influences and the plainspoken American songwriting tradition she draws from finally arrived at a fully formed voice of her own.

classicAlbums.title: Saint Cloud
classicAlbums.classicReason: Saint Cloud trades Waxahatchee's earlier lo-fi rock for a warmer, countryfied sound, pedal steel and organ filling in space where distortion used to sit. "Fire" turns a simple, repeated vow into the record's emotional center, Katie Crutchfield's voice steady and unguarded over a spare, twangy arrangement. The songwriting favors plainspoken directness over metaphor throughout, structured in short, direct verses that skip the conventional bridge almost entirely, trusting plain statement over ornament. It's the sound of a songwriter fully in command of the American tradition she draws from.

artists.name: Broken Social Scene
artists.bio:
Broken Social Scene formed in Toronto in 1999 around Kevin Drew and Brendan Canning as a loose, revolving collective rather than a fixed band, eventually drawing in more than twenty contributors across its recordings and shows, many of whom led their own separate projects. That collaborative, open-door structure became inseparable from the music itself, songs built up from whoever happened to be in the room rather than a single defined lineup.

You Forgot It in People, released in 2002, became the album most responsible for putting the collective on a wider map, and its reputation has only grown since: Pitchfork later named the band among the most important acts of the previous twenty-five years, and "Anthems for a Seventeen-Year-Old Girl" found a new audience after appearing in the film I Saw the TV Glow. Drew, asked to name his own favorite record, has pointed to Talk Talk's Laughing Stock and Dirty Three's Whatever You Love, You Are as tied for "the most authentic human emotion ever captured on an album" — fitting for a songwriter who later titled his own solo record Influences.

classicAlbums.title: You Forgot It in People
classicAlbums.classicReason: You Forgot It in People turns a revolving cast of more than twenty musicians into a single, cohesive wash of guitars, horns, and overlapping vocal lines, chaotic in personnel but never in execution. "Anthems for a Seventeen-Year-Old Girl" builds a hushed, elliptical verse into a swelling, wordless chorus that functions as pure catharsis rather than narrative. Elsewhere the record shifts from tender to raucous within a single track, treating its own unruliness as a virtue. It remains the clearest argument that a band built on chaos can still make something this unified.
classicAlbums.previewTrack: Anthems For A Seventeen Year-Old Girl

artists.previewTrack: Anthems For A Seventeen Year-Old Girl

artists.name: Drive-By Truckers
artists.bio:
Drive-By Truckers formed in Athens, Georgia in 1996, built around Patterson Hood and Mike Cooley after their earlier band, Adam's House Cat, broke up. Hood, the son of Muscle Shoals session bassist David Hood, grew up steeped in Southern musical history even as his own songwriting leaned toward the region's contradictions as much as its music; he has pointed to The Replacements and R.E.M. as the acts that shaped the band's earliest sound.

Southern Rock Opera, released in 2001, gave the band its first wide critical notice and established Hood and Cooley's songwriting partnership well before the shifting lineups that later included Jason Isbell and Spooner Oldham. Drive-By Truckers have continued recording and touring steadily since, built around Hood and Cooley's dual songwriting as the group's one constant through every other change, earning a reputation as one of American roots rock's most consistently respected working bands.

classicAlbums.title: Southern Rock Opera
classicAlbums.classicReason: Southern Rock Opera tackles Southern identity as a sprawling, self-aware concept record, using Lynyrd Skynyrd's story as scaffolding for a much wider argument about growing up in the region's contradictions. "Let There Be Rock" turns teenage devotion to arena rock into a genuine coming-of-age anthem, Patterson Hood and Mike Cooley's dual guitars and dual songwriting voices trading off without ever competing. The record never lets its historical ambition crowd out actual hooks. It remains the album that defined the band's mix of Southern-rock muscle and literary self-scrutiny.

artists.name: Lucinda Williams
artists.bio:
Lucinda Williams grew up immersed in literature before music, the daughter of poet and creative-writing teacher Miller Williams, who she has said gave her something "almost like an apprenticeship," with early critiques from family friends including poets James Dickey and John Ciardi and a literary diet that ran through Flannery O'Connor and Eudora Welty. A childhood encounter with Blind Pearly Brown, a street preacher she saw perform in Macon at age five, later became the subject of one of her own songs, and she has spoken about studying Bob Dylan specifically for his use of biblical stories and references.

Car Wheels on a Gravel Road, released in 1998 after a long, famously deliberate recording process, became her most widely heard record and the one that finally matched her singular songwriting to an audience well beyond the alt-country underground. Her influence on younger songwriters has continued since; Katie Crutchfield became a friend after interviewing her, one of many artists in the alt-country and confessional traditions to claim Williams as a direct reference point.

classicAlbums.title: Car Wheels on a Gravel Road
classicAlbums.classicReason: Car Wheels on a Gravel Road moves between country, blues, and rock without ever settling fully into any of them, Lucinda Williams's plainspoken, road-worn voice holding the shifting arrangements together. "Right in Time" turns a frank account of desire into one of the record's most disarming moments, its steady groove giving Williams room to sound both vulnerable and completely in control. The songwriting favors specific, physical detail over abstraction throughout. It remains the album most responsible for establishing her as a defining voice in modern American songwriting.

artists.previewAlbum: Car Wheels On a Gravel Road

artists.name: Devo
artists.bio:
Devo formed in Kent and Akron, Ohio, in 1973, art students led by Mark Mothersbaugh and Gerald Casale, built around a joke that wasn't quite one: de-evolution, the idea that humanity was going backwards. They played twitchy, robotic rock in matching jumpsuits, and their 1978 debut, produced by Brian Eno, made them leaders of new wave.

"Whip It" became a hit in 1980, but the early records are the ones other bands kept learning from: Pulp played "Gut Feeling" among their first songs. Mothersbaugh went on to score films and television.

classicAlbums.title: Q: Are We Not Men? A: We Are Devo!
classicAlbums.classicReason: Q: Are We Not Men? A: We Are Devo! turns rock into a nervous machine: choppy guitars, stiff robotic rhythms and Mark Mothersbaugh yelping like a man being rewired. "Gut Feeling" builds slowly from a chiming riff into a frantic rush, the band's tightest piece of tension and release. Brian Eno produced it, but the oddness is all theirs, down to a jerky, de-tuned cover of "(I Can't Get No) Satisfaction". It's the record that showed new wave could be smart, funny and unsettling at once.

artists.previewAlbum: Q: Are We Not Men? A: We Are Devo! (Deluxe Edition)

artists.name: King Crimson
artists.bio:
King Crimson formed in London in 1968 around guitarist Robert Fripp, and their first album the next year sounded like nothing else in rock: jazz-trained playing, mellotron orchestras, apocalyptic lyrics and sudden, violent loudness. Its opening song, "21st Century Schizoid Man", helped set the template for progressive rock, but the band never settled into it.

Fripp broke the lineup apart again and again, and each version reinvented the band: the improvising, heavy group of Larks' Tongues in Aspic and Red in the early 1970s, the interlocking guitars of Discipline in 1981, and more after. That restlessness is why they reach past prog: younger musicians from Wire's Colin Newman to Wilco's Nels Cline heard in them a band that would try anything.

classicAlbums.title: In the Court of the Crimson King
classicAlbums.classicReason: In the Court of the Crimson King opens with one of rock's great shocks: "21st Century Schizoid Man", a distorted vocal and a riff that lurches into frantic, jazz-speed runs played in unison. Then the record turns gentle, flute and mellotron carrying "I Talk to the Wind" and "Epitaph" into vast, mournful territory. The pull between brutality and beauty is the whole record. It's the album Colin Newman and Robert Pollard both name, years before either formed a band.

artists.previewAlbum: In the Court of the Crimson King (Expanded Edition)

artists.name: MC5
artists.bio:
MC5 formed in Detroit in 1964, a Lincoln Park high-school band built around guitarists Wayne Kramer and Fred "Sonic" Smith, drawing on garage rock and free jazz to make something louder and more chaotic than anything else in the city's rock clubs. Manager John Sinclair, a poet and co-founder of the White Panther Party, folded the band directly into his own revolutionary politics, turning gigs into rallies and its five members into reluctant spokesmen for a cause as much as for a sound.

Kick Out the Jams was recorded live at Detroit's Grande Ballroom over two nights in October 1968, before Elektra dropped the band the next year over the title track's language and its jab at a department store chain that had refused to stock the record. Vocalist Rob Tyner, drummer Dennis Thompson and bassist Michael Davis rounded out a lineup known locally for chaotic live shows before any label signed them. Sinclair's imprisonment and the White Panthers' collapse drained the momentum that had carried MC5, and the band dissolved within a few years. The Ramones later named MC5 first among their formative influences.

classicAlbums.title: Kick Out the Jams
classicAlbums.classicReason: Kick Out the Jams captures MC5 live at Detroit's Grande Ballroom, feedback and crowd noise bleeding straight into songs that barely stay inside their own arrangements. The title track opens on Rob Tyner's shouted rallying cry before Wayne Kramer and Fred "Sonic" Smith's dual guitars detonate into noise closer to free jazz than rock and roll. "Rocket Reducer No. 62" and "Starship" push the same chaos even further, the rhythm section barely holding each song together. It reads less like a studio statement than a document of a band trying to start a riot, and largely succeeding.

artists.name: Sex Pistols
artists.bio:
Sex Pistols formed in London in 1975 around a handful of young men who spent their afternoons at Malcolm McLaren and Vivienne Westwood's Kings Road boutique, SEX, McLaren shaping them into a calculated provocation as much as a band. Johnny Rotten's sneering vocal and Steve Jones's blunt, buzzsaw guitar gave the band a sound as confrontational as its lyrics, built to alarm a British public already primed to be scandalised by anything wearing a safety pin.

A June 1976 gig at Manchester's near-empty Lesser Free Trade Hall, organised by the fledgling Buzzcocks, became rock's most consequential forty-person audience: Bernard Sumner and Peter Hook left determined to start a band of their own, soon Joy Division. Sole studio album Never Mind the Bollocks, Here's the Sex Pistols followed in 1977, its shockwaves reaching a young Joe Strummer, who abandoned the 101ers days after his band opened for them, and reaching Bad Brains singer H.R. through a friend's record collection in Washington DC. The band collapsed on its first American tour in January 1978, barely three years after it began.

classicAlbums.title: Never Mind the Bollocks, Here's the Sex Pistols
classicAlbums.classicReason: Never Mind the Bollocks compresses two years of tabloid outrage into twelve songs that still sound genuinely dangerous rather than merely historic. "God Save the Queen" pairs Johnny Rotten's sneering, half-spoken vendetta against the monarchy with Steve Jones's thick, overdubbed guitar wall, released to coincide with the Queen's Silver Jubilee and promptly banned by the BBC. Producer Chris Thomas gave the band's chaos a hard, compact clarity most of their peers never bothered chasing. It remains the rare punk record whose reputation for danger the songs themselves still earn.

artists.previewAlbum: Never Mind the Bollocks, Here's the Sex Pistols

artists.name: Mary Timony
artists.bio:
Mary Timony started playing guitar in Washington DC's hardcore scene as a teenager, going to see Fugazi so often she later told The Hairpin she "went to every show they ever played," absorbing the tense, angular attack the scene prized. She co-founded Autoclave, a short-lived band on Dischord Records, before forming Helium in Boston in 1992, a band that spent the rest of the decade on Matador twisting Timony's fantasy-inflected lyrics and serpentine guitar lines into something closer to art-rock than the era's dominant slacker indie.

After Helium disbanded, Timony began a solo career that opened with Mountains in 2000, before she went on to co-found Wild Flag alongside Sleater-Kinney's Carrie Brownstein and later Ex Hex, carrying a guitar style that had grown steadily more direct without losing its underlying strangeness. Away from her own bands, she taught guitar lessons to a teenage Lindsey Jordan, who went on to record as Snail Mail and has credited Timony directly as a formative teacher rather than a mere influence.

classicAlbums.title: Mountains
classicAlbums.classicReason: Mountains, Timony's first record after Helium, trades that band's denser art-rock arrangements for something more spacious and exploratory, her guitar playing given room to wander into modal, almost medieval-sounding runs. "Dungeon Dance" rides a serpentine riff and hushed, incantatory vocal into a chorus that never quite resolves the tension it builds, closer to a spell than a pop song. The record's fantasy imagery and unhurried pacing set it apart from the more direct records that followed. It remains the clearest statement of Timony's own guitar language, unmediated by a band.

artists.name: Blood Orange
artists.bio:
Devonté Hynes grew up in Ilford, east London, and arrived first as a teenager in the dance-punk band Test Icicles before recasting himself as the orchestral folk act Lightspeed Champion. Blood Orange, begun in 2011 after he moved to New York, is the project where those reversals finally cohered — a producer's sensibility applied to soft-focus soul, with Hynes writing, playing and assembling most of the music himself while rotating guest vocalists through the frame. He has been explicit that the model for that structure is Massive Attack, one author and many voices, rather than any solo artist.

His stated influences run through British guitar music rather than the R&B lineage his sound is usually filed beside: the Smiths, Radiohead, New Order and Prefab Sprout, with Morrissey singled out for the bluntness of his lines. Freetown Sound (2016) and Negro Swan (2018) turned that inheritance toward questions of Black and queer identity, using spoken-word interludes and collage in place of conventional song structure. Alongside Blood Orange he has become one of the most sought-after writers and producers of his generation, though he keeps that work deliberately separate from the records released under his own project.

classicAlbums.title: Negro Swan
classicAlbums.classicReason: Negro Swan builds its songs out of quiet -- muted guitar figures, half-buried drum machines, and Devonté Hynes's voice sitting so low in the mix it often reads as an aside. "Charcoal Baby" is the album at its most direct, a clean guitar hook carrying a lyric about visibility and what it costs. Janet Mock's spoken interludes run through the record, framing it less as a song cycle than as a conversation about Black and queer interiority. The result is Hynes's warmest and most vulnerable album, built almost entirely out of restraint.

artists.name: Natural Snow Buildings
artists.bio:
Natural Snow Buildings are Mehdi Ameziane and Solange Gularte, a French duo who have worked in near-total isolation since 1998, releasing long, drone-heavy records in editions small enough that the music circulated mostly by reputation. Their sound sits between free folk and drone — acoustic guitar, bowed strings, harmonium and voice, recorded at home and allowed to run far past conventional album length. The pieces work less like songs than like weather systems, melodies surfacing out of the haze and receding back into it.

The duo are unusually resistant to naming influences. Asked directly, they have said their music is open to any influence, listing sources from France, Sudan, Ethiopia, India, the USA, Japan and Indonesia rather than a set of records. When they have named names, the list runs to Kath Bloom, Loren Mazzacane Connors, Neil Young, Six Organs of Admittance, Charalambides, Alice Coltrane and Stars of the Lid, with Fursaxa singled out as a genuine influence. The Winter Ray (2004) set the template — a self-released double album long enough to function as an environment — and The Dance of the Moon and the Sun (2006) is the record that carried it furthest and turned a hand-assembled CD-R operation into a cult concern. Most of that early catalogue has since been reissued digitally under the duo's own NSB Archive imprint.

classicAlbums.title: The Winter Ray
classicAlbums.classicReason: The Winter Ray is the duo's first sprawl on the scale they would become known for -- a self-released double album of twenty-five pieces that moves between two-minute fragments and seventeen-minute drones without ever changing its weather. Mehdi Ameziane and Solange Gularte record everything at home, and the tape hiss and room noise are part of the composition rather than a limitation of it. "Dead Horses" and "I Was Always Cold" are the long pieces the record is built around, while "Overture" and the title track work as the brief clearings between them. Issued in a tiny hand-assembled edition, it established the method every later Natural Snow Buildings record refines.

artists.name: The Breeders
artists.bio:
The Breeders began in 1989 as a side project for Kim Deal, then the bassist in Pixies, and Tanya Donelly of Throwing Muses, with Josephine Wiggs on bass and Slint's Britt Walford drumming under a pseudonym. Pod (1990), recorded by Steve Albini, established a sound built on Deal's plainspoken melodies and a rhythm section that treated space as an instrument. Kurt Cobain called it one of his favourite albums and singled out the way the songs were structured, and Deal has said she believes Pod is why Nirvana later hired Albini for In Utero.

By Last Splash (1993) the lineup had changed — Donelly had left to form Belly, and Deal's twin sister Kelley had joined on guitar — and the band became, briefly, a genuine commercial force. "Cannonball" went into heavy MTV rotation and the album went platinum, an outcome that sat awkwardly with a group whose instincts ran to the lopsided and the half-finished. Long silences followed, with Title TK (2002) and All Nerve (2018) arriving more than a decade apart, though the Last Splash lineup eventually reconvened and has held together since.

classicAlbums.title: Last Splash
classicAlbums.classicReason: Last Splash turns Kim Deal's gift for the deceptively simple hook loose over a rhythm section that never quite sits still, lurching between surf-rock, sludge and something close to pop. "Cannonball" is the one everyone knows -- built on a rubbery bassline and a distorted vocal intro that sounded like nothing else on 1993 radio -- but "Divine Hammer" and "Saints" work the same instinct at different speeds. Josephine Wiggs's bass carries more melody than most bands give their guitars. It remains the rare album that went platinum without smoothing away a single one of its odd edges.

artists.name: Mr. Bungle
artists.bio:
Mr. Bungle formed in Eureka, California, in 1985, high-school friends led by Mike Patton, Trey Spruance and Trevor Dunn. Patton's rise with Faith No More got them a major-label deal, and they used it to make records that lurch between funk metal, death metal, carnival music, jazz and lounge, often within one song.

Disco Volante (1995) and California (1999) are their most ambitious records, and their restless genre-switching shaped heavier bands that followed, the Dillinger Escape Plan among them, who opened for them on the California tour. They stopped in 2000, and came back in 2019 to re-record their early thrash demos.

classicAlbums.title: California
classicAlbums.classicReason: California sounds like a radio dial spun across fifty years: lounge, surf, exotica, doo-wop and sudden bursts of noise, each song switching style without warning. "Retrovertigo" is the calm at its centre, a sweeping, sincere ballad that Mike Patton sings completely straight. The production is lush and meticulous, which makes the sharp turns all the more startling. It's their most approachable record, and the one Ben Weinman says gave the Dillinger Escape Plan its thirst for diversity.

artists.name: Ween
artists.bio:
Ween formed in New Hope, Pennsylvania in 1984, when Aaron Freeman and Mickey Melchiondo met in an eighth-grade typing class and started recording on four-track as Gene and Dean Ween. The early records are deliberately abrasive lo-fi — pitch-shifted vocals, cheap drum machines, genre exercises pursued well past the point of the joke — and the band spent years filed as a novelty act on the strength of Pure Guava's "Push th' Little Daisies."

That reading undersold them badly. Dean Ween has described the band's foundation as the combined record collections he and Freeman grew up between, his own alongside Freeman's father's, which held everything from Nina Simone to the first two Velvet Underground albums to Captain Beefheart — "that's kind of what Ween is." From Chocolate and Cheese (1994) onward the craft caught up with the range, and by Quebec (2003) the parody instinct had largely given way to something more melancholy and direct. The band broke up in 2012 and reunited three years later.

classicAlbums.title: Quebec
classicAlbums.classicReason: Quebec is the record where Ween's parody instinct finally gives way to something closer to grief, the songs arriving warped but rarely winking. "Transdermal Celebration" is the clearest case -- a soaring, guitar-led melody set against imagery of environmental catastrophe and played entirely straight. Elsewhere the album swings between the woozy and the genuinely unsettling, held together by production that treats each genre exercise as a real song rather than a bit. It is the strongest argument that Ween were always a great band wearing a novelty band's clothes.
