scenes.name: No Wave
scenes.blurb: The scene born from the 1978 No New York compilation — abrasive, atonal, and deliberately hostile to rock convention — plus the guitar-orchestra wave of Glenn Branca and Rhys Chatham that grew up alongside it, with Swans emerging directly out of the same downtown scene.
placeAndTime: The scene's first tier lived in Lower Manhattan's loft and storefront circuit between 1976 and 1979 — cheap, unzoned spaces standing in for clubs, where DNA, Mars, Teenage Jesus and the Jerks, and James Chance and the Contortions played to the same few hundred people night after night. Brian Eno, in New York for other reasons, caught enough of it to produce No New York (1978), the compilation that gave the scene a name and a document for anyone who hadn't been in the room.

A second tier grew directly out of that milieu between 1979 and 1982: Glenn Branca and Rhys Chatham's massed-guitar ensembles, and Swans, formed by Michael Gira in 1982 out of the same downtown scene the compilation acts had defined. Branca's own label, Neutral Records, released Swans' debut album, Filth — the guitar-orchestra wing and the emerging noise-rock wing sharing not just a scene but a release schedule.

memberRoles.role: One of the four acts on No New York; Arto Lindsay and Ikue Mori's anti-technique approach set the scene's most structurally uncompromising benchmark.
Formed earliest of the compilation acts and pushed furthest from conventional rock; a Mars show was reportedly what sent Lydia Lunch off to start her own band.
Lydia Lunch's band, started after seeing Mars perform live; became the scene's most concentrated statement of deliberate ugliness and brevity.
Brought a trained funk rhythm section into the same rooms, giving the compilation its danceable, confrontational counterpoint to the other three acts' pure noise.

Formed in 1982 directly out of the downtown scene; Michael Gira called Branca's early concerts "the epitome of how high music can go," and the band's debut, Filth, came out on Branca's own Neutral Records.
Ran Neutral Records out of the same scene, releasing Swans' debut; had played in Rhys Chatham's Guitar Trio ensemble from 1977 to 1979 before building his own massed-guitar pieces.
Composed Guitar Trio (1977), the piece Branca played in before striking out on his own — the two composers' related but separate guitar-orchestra practices grew out of the same downtown room.

scenes.legacy: No New York's rejection of rock technique fed directly into noise rock and Sonic Youth's own guitar language, while Branca and Chatham's massed-guitar pieces shaped how a generation of post-rock and math-rock guitarists thought about tuning and repetition. Swans carried the scene's extremity forward for decades under its own name, long after the lofts that produced it were gone.

scenes.name: 4AD
scenes.blurb: Ivo Watts-Russell's London label built a shared gothic-ethereal house sound and, in This Mortal Coil, a literal label-artist collective drawing its lineup from the wider roster.
placeAndTime: 4AD was Ivo Watts-Russell's label from the outset, and by the early 1980s that meant something more specific than a shared roster: a deliberate house sound (reverbed, gothic, melancholic-but-beautiful) reinforced visually by Vaughan Oliver's sleeve designs under the name 23 Envelope, so that a 4AD record was identifiable by its cover before the needle ever dropped. Watts-Russell signed for a specific ear rather than a specific genre — Boston noise-pop (Pixies) sat on the same roster as Melbourne neoclassical duo Dead Can Dance — and the connective tissue was never sound so much as sensibility.

This Mortal Coil made that sensibility explicit. It was Watts-Russell's own project, not a band so much as a standing invitation to whoever was on the roster at the time — Cocteau Twins' Elizabeth Fraser and Robin Guthrie among them — to record other people's songs as chamber music. That a label could stage its own artists as a collective and have the results, most famously the cover of Tim Buckley's "Song to the Siren," read as a coherent artistic statement is the clearest evidence that 4AD in this period was a curated aesthetic community, not just a distribution deal.

memberRoles.role: Ivo Watts-Russell's own project — the label's curatorial ethos turned into an actual recording lineup, pulling in roster-mates like Cocteau Twins' Elizabeth Fraser and Robin Guthrie to record covers as 4AD house music.
The label's longest-serving flagship act and the clearest expression of its reverbed, ethereal house sound — the reference point every other 4AD signing got measured against.
Arrived later and closest to the exit into Britpop; Spooky (1992) was produced by Cocteau Twins' Robin Guthrie, carrying the house sound directly into Lush's own records.

Signed by Watts-Russell despite sounding nothing like the rest of the roster — Mark Kozelek's slowcore was shaped by the same atmospheres (This Mortal Coil, Cocteau Twins) even where the surface had none of their gloss.

The roster's outlier — loud, American, produced by Steve Albini in direct opposition to the label's reputation for gauze — signed by Watts-Russell anyway, proof the 4AD ear was never just a genre rule.

scenes.legacy: 4AD's house aesthetic outlived the label's original run, setting the visual and sonic template — Vaughan Oliver's sleeve art as much as the reverbed vocal sound — that dream-pop and shoegaze bands spent the following decade working from or against. This Mortal Coil in particular normalized the idea of a label as a creative collective rather than a distribution arrangement, a model since revisited by small labels wanting their signings to feel like one artistic project rather than a catalog.

scenes.name: DC Hardcore
scenes.blurb: A few dozen teenagers in Washington DC invented American hardcore's fastest music, its most durable independent label, and — without meaning to — a lifelong sobriety movement.
placeAndTime: Ian MacKaye and Jeff Nelson started Dischord Records as teenagers, simply to put out records by their own band and the handful of others playing the same small DC hardcore shows around them — a label built to document a scene its founders were already inside of, rather than to sign one from outside. That closeness meant the label's roster and the scene's actual social network were never really separate things: the same handful of musicians kept re-forming into new bands under the same label for well over a decade. Bad Brains, the band that set the whole thing moving, never released a record on Dischord at all — which is the clearest sign that the scene and the label were related but not identical.

The scene's furthest-travelling export left almost by accident. Minor Threat's "Straight Edge" (1981) runs under a minute and was written as one teenager's description of not drinking or taking drugs — a statement about himself, not a rule for anyone else. It was read as a manifesto anyway, and hardened into an international subculture with its own orthodoxy and its own enforcement, which Ian MacKaye spent the following decades explaining he had never meant to write. It is now better known than most of the music it came from.

memberRoles.role: MacKaye's band after Minor Threat, formed with Rites of Spring's Guy Picciotto and Brendan Canty and carrying Bad Brains' influence forward as the label's longest-running and most enduring act.
MacKaye and Nelson's first band, formed specifically to give Dischord something of their own to release, and the source of the scene's furthest-travelling export in a song called "Straight Edge".
Predated the DC scene and set it in motion — MacKaye's pre-Minor Threat band saw a Bad Brains show and came out transformed, and Picciotto later named them among Fugazi's own influences too.
Lasted barely a year, but its two core members, Picciotto and Canty, carried its emotionally raw "emocore" sound directly into Fugazi afterward.
Arrived a decade later out of the same Dischord-shaped DC underground, working in the post-hardcore vocabulary Fugazi and Bad Brains had already set down.

scenes.legacy: Dischord's insistence on five-dollar shows, no major-label deals, and total DIY control became the reference model for post-hardcore's entire operating ethic, and Fugazi in particular proved a serious touring band could run for decades entirely outside the industry's normal terms. The scene's other export travelled further and less deliberately: straight edge outgrew the record that named it, spread worldwide as a subculture with its own orthodoxy, and is now better known than most of the music it came from. Rites of Spring's short, emotionally raw run is the third line out of here, feeding the emo and post-hardcore realm this graph traces downstream.

scenes.name: SST Records
scenes.blurb: Greg Ginn's Los Angeles label turned hardcore into a distribution network for the country's furthest-out guitar music — a room as much as a roster.
placeAndTime: SST started as Greg Ginn's ham-radio parts mail-order business, run out of Hermosa Beach and San Pedro, before Ginn turned it into a record label for his own band, Black Flag. From there it became less a single room than an operation: Ginn signing and releasing bands he wanted to hear, then booking them onto shared bills and shared tours so a national hardcore circuit existed where none had before. Bands with no connection to Los Angeles at all — Hüsker Dü from Minneapolis, Sonic Youth from New York — plugged directly into that SST-run touring network alongside the label's own South Bay acts.

memberRoles.role: San Pedro locals and part of Ginn's own South Bay circle, touring the SST network constantly on almost no money alongside Black Flag.
Greg Ginn's own band and the reason the label existed in the first place; its relentless touring schedule set the operating template every other SST act followed.
Signed in from Minneapolis, plugging a Midwest band into a Los Angeles-run circuit and helping prove SST's network extended well past California.
South Bay labelmates connected to Black Flag directly through drummer Bill Stevenson's stint in that band, keeping the label's family of players tightly overlapping.

New York outsiders who toured the SST circuit despite no California roots; Lee Ranaldo has voiced admiration for Black Flag, more a mark of the label's camaraderie than a direct sound-influence claim.

scenes.legacy: SST's shared-bill touring model built the infrastructure American underground rock ran on for the rest of the 1980s, and its example — a working band's label distributing whatever else it wanted to hear — became the template college and indie labels followed afterward.

scenes.name: Riot Grrrl
scenes.blurb: The feminist punk movement that grew out of Olympia, Washington's cassette-and-zine DIY scene — Evergreen State College, K Records, and Kill Rock Stars all in the same small town.
placeAndTime: Olympia was a small state-capital college town built around Evergreen State College, an experimental school with no traditional grading system that drew exactly the kind of art-school-minded misfits who went on to start these bands. The town already had a functioning DIY music infrastructure before riot grrrl existed — Calvin Johnson's K Records had been putting out lo-fi, homemade records for years — and Kill Rock Stars emerged alongside the same scene as it grew, giving the movement a label of its own.

In a town this size, the scene was a handful of overlapping people playing the same small run of venues and house shows, trading zines as readily as they traded show flyers — the kind of close-quarters, everyone-knows-everyone network a town like Olympia could produce and a larger city couldn't.

memberRoles.role: Formed first, in 1990, out of Olympia's small DIY circuit — the band most identified with the scene that grew up around it.
Formed the following year when Allison Wolfe and Molly Neuman, already writing a zine together, started a band in the same town, running a parallel circuit alongside Bikini Kill.
Arrived in 1994, later than the other two, out of the same Olympia network; the band has since named both Bikini Kill and Bratmobile as direct influences.

scenes.legacy: Kill Rock Stars outlasted the movement itself to become a lasting indie label, and Olympia's small-town, zine-and-cassette model of self-organizing a scene became a template later DIY punk and indie circuits consciously imitated.

scenes.name: Bristol
scenes.blurb: A downtempo, bass-heavy sound built out of the same Bristol sound systems and studios, blending hip-hop, dub, and soul into what critics later called trip-hop.
placeAndTime: Massive Attack's founding members came directly out of the Wild Bunch, a loose Bristol DJ-and-MC sound system that had been playing hip-hop, dub, and soul to local crowds through the mid-1980s before splintering into several separate projects once it dissolved. Bristol's relationship to that music wasn't an import — the city's long-standing Caribbean immigrant community had supported sound-system culture for years before any of these acts existed, and it's that infrastructure, not a studio or a label, that the scene actually grew out of.

The three acts here stayed genuinely local and interconnected rather than just regionally adjacent: Geoff Barrow worked as a tape-op on Massive Attack's Blue Lines sessions and used the spare studio hours he was given there to start Portishead, and Tricky — another Wild Bunch alumnus — rapped on Blue Lines and Protection before going solo. Plenty of later acts named these records as the reason they sounded the way they did, but naming an influence is not the same as having been in the room, and only the ones who were are listed here.

memberRoles.role: Formed from the wreckage of the Wild Bunch sound system and became the scene's hub — nearly every other act here either grew directly out of their sessions or named them as the reason they started.

Geoff Barrow worked as a tape-op on Massive Attack's Blue Lines sessions and used the spare studio time he was given there to build his own project — the clearest line of direct, practical descent in the whole scene.
A Wild Bunch member in his own right before Massive Attack existed under that name; rapped on Blue Lines and Protection before leaving to make Maxinquaye alone.

scenes.legacy: The Bristol sound left the city with a genre name it never asked for — critics called it trip-hop, a term Massive Attack in particular has always resisted — but the slow tempos, dub bass, and cinematic sampling defined here shaped downtempo and electronic pop internationally for the rest of the decade. Portishead's own eleven-year gap between their second album and Third (2008) became its own kind of template: a scene that never needed to stay prolific to stay influential.

scenes.name: CBGB
scenes.blurb: Hilly Kristal's Bowery dive booked bands on one condition — play your own songs — and four groups who sounded nothing alike built American punk out of that single rule.
placeAndTime: CBGB opened at 315 Bowery in 1973 under Hilly Kristal and his ex-wife Karen, named for the country, bluegrass and blues he intended to book and never really did. The room was long, narrow and filthy, on a stretch of the Bowery nobody else wanted, and what made it matter was not its stage but its booking policy: from early 1974 Kristal would take almost any band provided they played original material. The rule was partly idealism and partly economics — covers meant paying performance royalties — and its effect was to filter for the only thing these bands had in common, which was having written something themselves.

That policy is why the room produced no house sound. Television's guitar interplay owed more to Coltrane than to rock and roll, the Ramones played two-minute songs at one volume, Patti Smith was a poet who had backed into a band, and Talking Heads were art students studying the form from the outside. They shared a stage, a bar and an audience for about three years, and almost nothing else.

memberRoles.role: Queens four-piece who took the original-material rule to its logical extreme — two-minute songs, one tempo, no solos — and toured the UK in 1976 in front of the musicians who would form the Sex Pistols and the Clash.
Arrived in the Bowery in 1974 and effectively opened the room to rock bands; Marquee Moon (1977) is the scene's least punk record and its most technically ambitious.
Came to the stage from poetry rather than from bands, and her 1975 residency with Television is what turned a bar with a booking policy into a scene people travelled to see.

Art-school outsiders who played their first proper gig here in 1975; David Byrne has recounted Johnny Ramone handing them an opening slot with the endorsement "Sure, they're gonna suck, so no problem."

scenes.legacy: Almost nothing connects these four musically, and that is the point: the Ramones' own drummer drew a line between his CBGB peers and the bands that actually influenced him, so on the map no line of influence joins most of them. What they shared was a room and a rule, and each left it in a different direction — the Ramones into punk, Television into art rock, Smith into poetry-as-performance, Talking Heads into art-pop and eventually Remain in Light. The scene's descendants are enormous and almost entirely separate from one another.

scenes.name: Düsseldorf–Cologne
scenes.blurb: Two Rhineland cities forty kilometers apart, one producer's farmhouse studio, and a set of bands who decided post-war German music should not sound American.
placeAndTime: This was never a single venue. Can formed in Cologne in 1968 around two Stockhausen students and built their own studio; Kraftwerk formed in Düsseldorf in 1970; Neu! formed in Düsseldorf in 1971 when Klaus Dinger and Michael Rother left an early Kraftwerk lineup. The cities are about forty kilometers apart, and the scene was that corridor rather than any one room — a generation with no interest in reproducing Anglo-American blues rock, working out what German music could sound like instead.

The closest thing to a shared room was Conny Plank's studio on a farm outside Cologne. Plank engineered every Neu! recording and Kraftwerk's first four albums, and the scene's window closes where his involvement does: Autobahn (1974) was the last Kraftwerk record he worked on, after which the band moved into its own Kling Klang studio and out of everyone else's orbit.

memberRoles.role: Started as one more long-form Düsseldorf experiment and left as something else entirely; Autobahn (1974) both ends this scene and begins the lineage most of the map's electronic side descends from.

Formed by two musicians who had just left Kraftwerk — the scene's one hard personnel link — and built the motorik beat that Dinger described as a way of removing everything decorative from rock drumming.
The Cologne end of the corridor and the oldest of the three, working from a conservatoire background rather than a rock one, with a rhythm section precise enough to make improvisation sound composed.

scenes.legacy: Everything downstream of this corridor arrived by a different route than the bands intended: Neu!'s motorik became the default rhythm of post-punk and indie, Can's rhythm section became a permanent reference for anyone building songs out of repetition, and Kraftwerk's machines were picked up first by Detroit techno and the Bronx rather than by anyone in Europe. All three sit at the centre of this map, and nearly all of its electronic side descends from them.

scenes.name: Greenwich Village
scenes.blurb: A few square blocks of Manhattan coffeehouses where the songs belonged to everybody and the performers were judged on what they could do with them.
placeAndTime: The Village folk revival ran on rooms that barely qualified as venues — coffeehouses and basket houses around MacDougal and Bleecker where performers were paid from a basket passed around the audience, if at all. The circuit was small enough that everyone played the same handful of rooms and watched each other do it, and its repertoire was largely traditional and shared: the same songs moved from singer to singer, so a performance was measured by interpretation rather than authorship. That is what made it a scene rather than a set of solo careers, and it is also what made it fragile — once writing your own material became the point, the shared songbook that held it together stopped mattering.

memberRoles.role: Arrived in New York in 1961 steeped in Woody Guthrie and spent five years outgrowing the revival that made him, plugging in for Highway 61 Revisited in 1965 while parts of the folk audience treated it as a betrayal.

The singer Dylan singled out as his favorite in the Village, and the one who left least behind — she mistrusted recording, sang other writers' songs rather than her own, and made both her albums somewhat against her own wishes.

scenes.legacy: The revival's most famous participant spent the rest of the decade dismantling it, and the interpretive tradition it ran on — take a song someone else wrote and make it yours — receded as songwriting became the measure of a folk artist. Dalton is the clearer inheritance: her cracked, jazz-inflected phrasing found its audience decades late, and the confessional and freak-folk lineages this graph traces run through singers who found her long after the Village had gone.

scenes.name: The Windmill Scene
scenes.blurb: Since 2016, a run of art-literate, genre-restless bands has converged on one small Brixton pub venue — the Windmill — where a permissive booker and a rotating cast of overlapping members turned a 150-capacity room into a genuine incubator, still active today.
placeAndTime: The Windmill isn't a genre venue — it's a Brixton pub room that will book almost anything, run by promoters willing to give unsigned, half-formed bands a regular slot and an audience that's mostly other musicians. That informality, more than any shared sound, is what let a small circle of acts trade members, ideas, and stage time for years before any of them had a record deal.

The bands that came out of it share almost no fixed genre — jazz-inflected post-punk, glitchy chamber-pop, motorik dance-punk, prog-scrambled art-rock — but they share the room, overlapping lineups, and a wave of press attention that landed on all of them at once around 2019 and hasn't really let up since.

memberRoles.role: The scene's most sonically extreme act and, by reputation, its center of gravity — their controlled-chaos live sets became the thing other Windmill regulars measured their own gigs against.

Formed a couple of years after black midi out of an earlier band's remnants, and became stage-mates and label-mates rather than direct followers — Georgia Ellery's parallel membership in Jockstrap tied the two bands together directly.

The one act here that didn't start in London — met at university in Brighton and only became part of this scene once they relocated and started playing the same stage as black midi and Black Country, New Road.

Formed out of the Guildhall School rather than the Windmill circuit itself, but Georgia Ellery's parallel membership in Black Country, New Road made the two bands' overlap concrete rather than just a shared bill.

scenes.legacy: Mercury Prize nominations for black midi and Black Country, New Road, and wide critical attention for Squid and Jockstrap, took the scene from a single pub circuit to an internationally covered story within a couple of years. It's too recent to say yet what these bands will go on to influence — the more honest claim is just how fast a 150-capacity room turned into an internationally-watched scene.

scenes.name: Manchester
scenes.blurb: The Manchester scene that grew out of the Sex Pistols' 1976 Free Trade Hall gigs, producing post-punk's two defining tonal opposites in Joy Division and The Fall alongside pop-punk's Buzzcocks.
placeAndTime: On June 4, 1976, the Sex Pistols played a poorly attended gig at Manchester's Free Trade Hall that Buzzcocks had organized and booked themselves onto as support — a booking made on the strength of a single NME review and a trip down to London to persuade the band to come north. The audience was small, but its legend has only grown since: a disproportionate number of the people in that room went on to form the bands that defined Manchester post-punk over the following five years.

Tony Wilson, a Granada TV presenter who was in the Free Trade Hall audience himself, formed Factory Records a couple of years later and signed Joy Division — turning the loose, gig-sparked scene into something with an actual institutional home, a label rather than just a shared origin story.

memberRoles.role: Formed later that same year by musicians who were present, or said to have been present, at the Free Trade Hall show — the gig's most direct and most mythologized consequence.

Formed the same year as Joy Division, out of the same city and moment, but built around Mark E. Smith's contempt for conventional structure into post-punk's other tonal pole — abrasive where Joy Division was austere.
The connective tissue for the whole scene — organized and played the gig that started it, before Pete Shelley steered the band itself toward faster, stranger pop-punk once Howard Devoto left.

scenes.legacy: The Free Trade Hall gig became one of British music's most-cited origin stories, and Joy Division's Martin Hannett-produced records set an emotional and sonic template — for post-punk's interiority, later for shoegaze's — that outlasted the scene itself by decades. Factory Records gave the slightly later Manchester scene its institutional home and, in Joy Division's afterlife as New Order, its own separate second act.

scenes.name: Elephant 6
scenes.blurb: A loose collective of psychedelic-pop bands who started in Denver before relocating to Athens, Georgia, sharing members, home-recording gear, and a shared four-track ethos.
placeAndTime: Jeff Mangum, Bill Doss, Will Cullen Hart, and Robert Schneider grew up together as friends in Ruston, Louisiana, absorbing the same Beatles and Beach Boys records before scattering and regrouping first in Denver and then in Athens, Georgia, where the loose collective took the Elephant 6 Recording Company name. What held the group together wasn't a shared address so much as shared equipment and method — four-track home recording passed between members' bedrooms rather than time booked in a commercial studio.
Robert Schneider produced across much of the collective's catalog, a circumstance of how Elephant 6 pooled its limited resources rather than a case of him influencing the other bands' sound.

memberRoles.role: Jeff Mangum, one of the original Ruston friends, moved to Athens specifically to be near the rest of the collective before recording as Neutral Milk Hotel.
Kevin Barnes joined the collective later, in Athens, after it had already relocated there — not one of the original Ruston friends, but folded into the same circle once he arrived.
Bill Doss and Will Cullen Hart, both original Ruston friends alongside Mangum, pushed the collective's more experimental, tape-collage wing furthest.

scenes.legacy: In the Aeroplane Over the Sea's slow rediscovery turned Elephant 6's bedroom four-track aesthetic into a direct reference point for a later generation of indie bands, including members of Arcade Fire and the Shins, while Olivia Tremor Control's studio abstraction found later admirers in acts as large as Radiohead and the Flaming Lips.

scenes.name: Seattle
scenes.blurb: The Sub Pop-adjacent grunge scene at the turn of the '90s, alongside the more melodic, off-kilter emo of Sunny Day Real Estate working the same clubs.
placeAndTime: Sub Pop was the connective institution: a shoestring local label that put out Mudhoney's and Nirvana's earliest records and, through its own grimy Pacific Northwest branding, gave a loose cluster of Seattle-area bands a shared identity before they had much else in common. The city's club circuit was small enough that bands working in entirely different registers — Sub Pop's grunge acts and a post-hardcore-schooled band like Sunny Day Real Estate, also on the label — played the same rooms to the same audiences without belonging to the same sound at all.

memberRoles.role: Formed in nearby Aberdeen and folded into the Seattle scene through Sub Pop, which released Bleach before the band left the city's orbit entirely with Nevermind.
One of Sub Pop's first signings and the clearest early document of the label's fuzzed-out house sound; Kurt Cobain named them his favorite band.
Signed to Sub Pop just as its grunge-defined identity was shifting, playing the same Seattle circuit as the city's grunge bands while sounding nothing like them.

scenes.legacy: Nirvana's breakout took the Sub Pop sound global almost overnight and effectively ended grunge's run as an underground genre, while Sunny Day Real Estate's members carried the city's other current forward — into Foo Fighters and into what would become second-wave emo.

scenes.name: Detroit–Ann Arbor
scenes.blurb: A Detroit ballroom and an Ann Arbor commune, where the MC5 were the house band and the Stooges were their little brothers, until one record-label trip in 1968 signed them both.
placeAndTime: The Grande Ballroom opened in Detroit on 7 October 1966, to about sixty people, with the MC5 on the bill, and the band became its anchor, playing there at least once a week. Their manager, John Sinclair, ran Trans-Love Energies, a commune that moved in May 1968 to a big house at 1510 Hill Street in Ann Arbor. For a while the Stooges counted as a Trans-Love band too; they lived across town in their own band house on Packard Road, the Fun House their second album is named after. Sinclair recommended them to the Grande's owner, Russ Gibb, and they first played there in January 1968, on a bill headed by John Mayall.

The two bands met their record label on the same weekend. In September 1968 Elektra's Danny Fields flew in to hear the MC5, at the Grande and at a benefit in Ann Arbor's Union Ballroom where the Stooges were playing too; Fields has said Wayne Kramer told him that if he liked the MC5 he'd like their little brother band. Elektra signed both on 26 September, the Stooges for $5,000 as the small half of what Fields called a package deal. The room came apart within a year: Elektra dropped the MC5 in April 1969, the band left Sinclair's politics that June, and in July, days after both bands played a benefit for him at the Grande, Sinclair went to prison.

memberRoles.role: The Grande's house band from its opening night, managed by John Sinclair, and the band that recorded its debut, Kick Out the Jams, live in that room over two nights in October 1968.
The MC5's little brother band, who opened for them and reached Elektra on Wayne Kramer's tip; their band house on Packard Road, the Fun House, gave their second album its name.

scenes.legacy: The Rock and Roll Hall of Fame calls the Stooges "punk before punk existed" and credits the MC5 with creating its template, and the Ramones named the MC5 first among their influences. The Stooges' first album was produced by John Cale of the Velvet Underground; on this map the bands that name the Stooges run from the Ramones and Joy Division to Black Flag.

scenes.name: Lower East Side
scenes.place: Lower East Side and East Village, New York
scenes.blurb: A handful of small bars around Ludlow Street and an East Village dance label, where guitar bands and DJs shared the same rooms just before the world came looking.
placeAndTime: The rooms were small and a few streets apart: the Mercury Lounge on Houston Street, Luna Lounge on Ludlow, Brownies on Avenue A. The Strokes played their first gig in 1999 and spent 2000 on residencies at the Mercury Lounge and the Bowery Ballroom; the Mercury's junior booker, Ryan Gentles, booked them that August and left the club to become their manager. The Yeah Yeah Yeahs played their first show at the Mercury Lounge in September 2000, opening for the White Stripes with their drummer on Meg White's kit, and Interpol found their footing at Brownies and at Luna Lounge, whose co-owner Rob Sacher booked them.

A few blocks away the other half of the scene ran on records. James Murphy and Tim Goldsworthy's DFA made records in their Plantain studio on West 13th Street, and Murphy DJ'd at Plant Bar in the East Village; he first saw the Rapture at a gig at Brownies in 1999, and DFA found them places to live and jobs at Plant Bar. Sharing rooms didn't make them a gang: Paul Banks has said the Strokes were hanging out in exactly the same places he was, and he didn't know any of them. In 2003 a compilation put the Strokes, the Yeah Yeah Yeahs, Interpol, the Rapture and LCD Soundsystem on one record and called it Yes New York, after No New York. Luna Lounge closed in June 2005.

memberRoles.role: Played their first gig in 1999 and spent 2000 on Mercury Lounge residencies, taking the club's booker with them as their manager; the first of these bands to break, with Is This It in 2001.
Debuted at the Mercury Lounge in September 2000, opening for the White Stripes, and became a Brownies favourite; by Paul Banks's account, Nick Zinner knew people in Interpol and was part of a scene.
Learned to play live at Brownies and Luna Lounge, booked by Rob Sacher; Paul Banks says the Strokes were hanging out in exactly the same places he was, and he didn't know any of them.

Came east from San Francisco by way of Seattle, were spotted by James Murphy at Brownies, and made "House of Jealous Lovers" with DFA in 2002, the single that put this scene's guitars on the dance floor.

Here as James Murphy before it was a band: DFA's producer and Plant Bar DJ, who made "Losing My Edge" in the Plantain studio. LCD Soundsystem played its first show as a band in London, in November 2002.

scenes.legacy: NME named Is This It the album of the decade in 2009, and its short songs and two guitars became the default shape of a guitar band for years afterwards. "House of Jealous Lovers" started a run of New York dance-punk that LCD Soundsystem carried furthest, all the way to a farewell at Madison Square Garden in 2011.

scenes.name: PC Music
scenes.blurb: A.G. Cook's label was really a circle of school and university friends, with SOPHIE alongside, putting out exaggerated, candy-bright pop almost every week, then making Charli XCX's records.
placeAndTime: A.G. Cook started PC Music in June 2013, around the time he graduated from Goldsmiths, and built it around people he already knew. Danny L Harle was an old school friend he met again at university; Gus Lobban, who recorded as Kane West, was a year below him at Goldsmiths; Polly-Louisa Salmon, who made records as GFOTY, was a school friend. Hannah Diamond, a former fashion and styling student who had co-founded LOGO Magazine, easyFun, Lil Data and felicita completed the circle. Caroline Polachek called it "a collective of friends" that "clearly wasn't a label in the conventional sense." From 2014 to 2015 it put out new music almost every week.

It had rooms as well as release dates. On 24 January 2014 SOPHIE and Cook played the basement of Power Lunches in Dalston, and that April Hannah Diamond gave her first live show at the Edition Hotel in central London. SOPHIE never technically signed to the label, but she worked inside the circle: with Cook, the singer Harriet Pittard and Hayden Dunham she was part of QT, whose "Hey QT" came out on XL Recordings in August 2014. From 2016 the circle's biggest room was Charli XCX's records: SOPHIE produced her Vroom Vroom EP that February, Cook became her creative director late that year, and Pop 2 (December 2017), made with him, SOPHIE, easyFun and Lil Data, was recorded mostly in Alicia Keys' old New York studio, with other sessions in London.

memberRoles.role: Started PC Music in June 2013 with school and Goldsmiths friends and ran it through the Columbia deal, then became Charli XCX's creative director in late 2016. He still hears SOPHIE's fingerprints on his later records.

A close associate who never technically signed to PC Music: she played the Power Lunches basement with Cook in January 2014 and was part of QT with him, whose "Hey QT" came out on XL Recordings in August 2014.
Never on the label, but from 2016 the circle made her records: SOPHIE produced her Vroom Vroom EP, and Cook, her creative director, executive-produced Pop 2 (2017) with SOPHIE, easyFun and Lil Data.

scenes.legacy: The sound later filed under hyperpop reached the wider world through Pop 2, which Pitchfork called "the best full-length work of both Charli and PC Music's respective careers," and through SOPHIE, whom Charli named at the 2025 BRIT Awards as someone "none of us would be up here without." PC Music itself put out new music until 2023 and has released only archival records since. On this map Slayyyter and Ninajirachi name SOPHIE as an influence, and Cook traces his own influences back to Kraftwerk.

edges.citation: David Byrne to Rolling Stone on Lou Reed's death (2013): "his music, with and without the Velvets, was a big influence on myself and Talking Heads." He added: "His work and that of the Velvets was a big reason I moved to NY."

David Byrne on BBC Desert Island Discs (2018), as reported by Far Out, picking the Stooges' "I Wanna Be Your Dog": the band came "from somewhere you didn't know existed"; he and the rest of Talking Heads were listening to the Stooges alongside a lot of R&B while forming the band.

Far Out Magazine: "Frantz also revealed that all of the Talking Heads members loved the Ramones even though their punk contemporaries didn't initially enjoy their brand of 'new wave' but eventually were won over."
Ultimate Classic Rock, reporting David Byrne's Pitchfork interview (2023): the Byrds helped Byrne move on from folk, and David Bowie and the Velvet Underground "provided his next steps".

Peter Hook to Denver Westword (2 Sept 2022), on Ian Curtis educating him musically: "He'd give me Velvet Underground Loaded, and he'd give me a John Cale solo album. Then he'd do Can and Faust and Kraftwerk."
Paul Lester, The Guardian (31 Aug 2007), on the film Control: the story begins with the 17-year-old Ian Curtis "dreaming of David Bowie, Iggy Pop and Lou Reed."

Robert Smith, asked how Bowie influenced his approach to music, as quoted by Far Out: "David Bowie was probably the first artist that I felt was mine. He was singing to me." Ziggy Stardust was the first vinyl album he bought.
Michael Bracewell, "Her dark materials," The Guardian (24 Sept 2005), calls the Velvet Underground and Roxy Music the band's "musical heroes."

Siouxsie Sioux, foreword to MOJO's David Bowie special edition (dated November 2003): "I was 15 when I first saw David Bowie... I just couldn't believe how striking he was... It was no coincidence that so many people involved in punk at the beginning had been inspired by him. Bowie was the catalyst who'd brought a lot of us, the so-called Bromley Contingent, together. And out of that really small group of people, a lot happened including Siouxsie And The Banshees."

Johnny Marr of The Smiths, choosing The Velvet Underground's VU for The Quietus's Baker's Dozen: "I played 'I Can't Stand It' so many times that it stuck in my subconscious and that came out as the inspiration for the rhythm part on the song 'The Queen Is Dead'."

Morrissey, the Smiths' singer, became a glam rock fan in the 1970s, enjoying the work of English artists such as T. Rex, David Bowie and Roxy Music (David Bret, Morrissey: Scandal and Passion, Robson Books, 2004, p. 15).
edges.sourcePrint: David Bret, Morrissey: Scandal and Passion (Robson Books), 2004, p. 15

edges.citation: Jon King to the Pocklington Post: seeing the Velvet Underground was "really a pilgrimage because The Velvet Underground was really the marker for me and Andy of what bands should sound like and we came back and thought we'd have a band."

Nick Cave, in his Channel 4 tribute after Lou Reed's death (2013), as reported by Why Now: "He taught me that you can put the most sonically aggressive music and put it side by side with some of the most beautiful ballads that anyone has ever written."
Rolling Stone, on writing Psychocandy: "we got seriously into the Velvets and the Stooges."

Martin Aston, in MOJO's sidebar to his Robin Guthrie interview (December 2011), reproduced on the band's site, wrote that "Pearly-Dewdrops' Drops" "saw them discard their earlier Siouxsie & The Banshees influences to reveal a unique musical intricacy."

Robin Guthrie to Martin Aston, MOJO (December 2011), on what he listened to before forming the band: "I liked all the early punk—Buzzcocks, the Pistols and The Clash, before it all went commercial." The band set out "to make music with the energy of punk but with more finesse and beauty."

Robin Guthrie to Martin Aston, MOJO (December 2011), reposted on the band's site: "I adored the fast R&B of Doctor Feelgood and The Count Bishops, and then I heard the Ramones. Punk spoke to me even more because it was new whereas R&B was revivalist."

Hope Sandoval to The Quietus: "He knew more about the Velvet Underground; I didn't really know their music... But when I started working with David, he turned me on to them." Her bandmate David Roback was the one who knew the Velvet Underground.

Kevin Shields told Mixdown (2024) that The Jesus and Mary Chain's first single, along with Einstürzende Neubauten's live show, was among the things pulling My Bloody Valentine towards their early direction, though he called the idea of a shared Cocteau Twins and Jesus and Mary Chain influence "garbage" and named Psychocandy as the one shared record.

Kevin Shields to Hua Hsu, Arthur No. 7 (Nov. 2003), on the Ramones and Johnny Ramone's guitar: "And that's what happened—that's the Ramones connection. What I did that was any good in the end came from the mentality that Johnny wasn't playing guitar."
Kevin Shields to Hua Hsu in Arthur (2003), on the first Creation session: "It was good because we were letting ourselves be more Sonic Youth-y, more of our influences in a way."
Neil Halstead to Reverb (2017): "When I listened to My Bloody Valentine and Cocteau Twins I wanted something between those sounds."
Neil Halstead to Under the Radar (2014): "We'd all drive around endlessly in Nick's car — because he was the only one of us who had a car — and listen to tapes of Cocteau Twins albums."
Andy Bell to Premier Guitar: "My Bloody Valentine was hugely influential on the bass sound... We had become addicted to noise."
Emma Anderson to Flood (2016): "I was all about post-punk. I liked the Cocteau Twins and Siouxsie and the Banshees."

Bradford Cox of Deerhunter, choosing Broadcast's Tender Buttons for The Quietus's Baker's Dozen: "it had a huge effect on me. There was this unfinished quality to it, that I learned from. And it's really what pushed me to actually start a band with Moses"

Roberto Burgos to Jesse Taconelli, "Sonemic Interview: Sweet Trip" (December 2020), on coming to indie rock from heavy metal: "it was a brave new world – Sonic Youth, The Stone Roses, My Bloody Valentine, Slowdive – and these bands made me feel so much, like eating Gouda for the first time and never going back to American cheese."

Valerie Cooper of Sweet Trip, in a Sonemic interview with Rate Your Music, choosing Cocteau Twins' Lorelei among the band's album inspirations: "How to sing like a pro and make everyone fall in love with you or let you fall in love with all of them."
Jellybones: "as I became influenced by Takagi Masakatsu, Sufjan Stevens, and Sweet Trip, I wanted to put all my favorite things into one album."
Jellybones: "as I became influenced by Takagi Masakatsu, Sufjan Stevens, and Sweet Trip, I wanted to put all my favorite things into one album."

Joey Santiago to Film Score Monthly (2003), on learning guitar: his brother "had the Velvet Underground's Loaded on his turntable. I played it and learned the song 'Rock and Roll.' It had this soaring guitar at the breaks, very simple, very effective. That hooked me."
Wikipedia's Black Francis article: Kim Deal joined Pixies through a classified advertisement in a Boston paper that asked for a bassist "into Hüsker Dü and Peter, Paul and Mary".

Thurston Moore to PBS American Masters (interview dated 13 July 1997): he met his first New York bandmate J.D. King while browsing the Velvet Underground bin of a New Haven record store, and of Sonic Youth he says "We never really wanted to sound like the Velvet Underground. We just sort of wanted to use elements of what they were doing as, again, just sort of carry on that lineage."

Lee Ranaldo, in Pitchfork's 5-10-15-20 (2012): "At the time, that was very important to my re-involvement with music, which had gotten so bombastic, serving larger audiences and scenes and big stadium concerts."

J Mascis in MOJO's Dinosaur Jr. oral history (May 2021): "We loved the Minutemen, Hüsker Dü and the Meat Puppets, and our ambition was to tour like they did and sign to SST Records, the label they were on."

Lou Barlow in the oral history Dinosaur Jr. by Dinosaur Jr., excerpted by SPIN (2014): "I was in awe of Sonic Youth and could barely talk to them". J Mascis recalls of the drive home from their first tour together, listening to Sonic Youth's EVOL: "I almost feel like crying. I think we're in love with Sonic Youth."

J Mascis in MOJO's Dinosaur Jr. oral history (May 2021): "We loved the Minutemen, Hüsker Dü and the Meat Puppets, and our ambition was to tour like they did and sign to SST Records, the label they were on."
Wikipedia's Dinosaur Jr. article: after high school, Mascis and Barlow began exploring slower yet still aggressive music like Black Sabbath, the Replacements and Neil Young.
Paul Westerberg sings it in the Replacements' "Alex Chilton" (1987), named for Big Star's singer: "I never travel far without a little Big Star."
Wikipedia's article on the band says the Replacements' music was influenced by punk rock bands including the Ramones, the New York Dolls, the Buzzcocks, the Damned and the Sex Pistols.

Bob Nastanovich to The A.V. Club (2022), on touring with Sonic Youth: "we all got along well, and were huge fans. EVOL and Sister changed my life, and 'The World Looks Red' is my favorite Sonic Youth song."
Stephen Malkmus told The Observer in 2013 (reported by NME) that the Velvet Underground's "Sister Ray" is "the ultimate song... It is with me always."

Jim Greer in SPIN (1994) writes that Pavement's "Unseen Power of the Picket Fence" is "a paean to the Athens, Georgia, combo, and specifically to Reckoning." The A.V. Club (2022) also calls R.E.M. among Pavement's "own heroes."
The Michigan Daily (30 Nov 1995) says Yo La Tengo have been recognised as deeply influenced by the Velvet Underground, and that Ira Kaplan acknowledges having always been a big fan of the band.

Ira Kaplan to Premier Guitar, asked how much bands like Big Star changed the way he thought about guitar: "At that point, I started tracking down Big Star's music, getting copies of #1 Record and Radio City, and then I snapped up Third when it came out."

Peter Buck of R.E.M. to Yahoo Music (November 2014), on the band's early Velvet Underground covers: "That was stuff we loved... 'There She Goes' and 'Pale Blue Eyes'... fit in pretty well with what we were doing at the time and they did influence a lot."
Michael Stipe, in Pitchfork's 5-10-15-20 (2021): "I had this epiphany and realized that this is what I wanted to do with my life: learn how to sing and start a band."

Stipe, in Stereogum's "80 Artists Pick Their Favorite Neil Young Song": he never listened to Young much himself, but Young was a favorite of all the guys in the band, "especially Peter" -- one of the main reasons they signed to Warner Bros.
Colin Greenwood to The Big Issue (2024), on his brother Jonny: "He could play the keyboards and then he learned the guitar very quickly, listening to Pixies and Lou Reed's New York album."

Thom Yorke, quoted by Far Out Magazine, on Remain in Light: "It was like a bomb going off in my head; I'd literally never heard anything like it... Talking Heads did something with a studio that had never been done before. And even at a young age, I could see that."

Thom Yorke to VinylWriters, as quoted by Far Out: "Then I discovered R.E.M. and it turned my life upside down." He added: "Shortly after that, I signed up for art school and started to take making music seriously."

Wikipedia, citing John Robb's The Stone Roses and the Resurrection of British Pop (Random House, 2001, pp. 154-155): in 1986 the band's songs such as "Sugar Spun Sister" were "influenced by bands like the Jesus & Mary Chain and the indie-pop era Primal Scream".

edges.citation: BBC News, "The Smiths: the influential alliance": "Marr's guitar style was a huge building block for more Manchester legends that followed The Smiths - The Stone Roses, with their guitarist John Squire acknowledging the debt he owed to Marr."

Ian Brown, in the Observer's Soundtrack of My Life (2010): of The Clash's first album, which he played John Squire: "he went and bought it the next day, and played it every day for about 18 months, before and after school. That got him obsessed with guitar and made him want to play."

Julian Casablancas to Rolling Stone (2003): the dream when they formed the Strokes "revolved around taking the Velvet Underground and thinking, 'If only they were really famous.'" The seed of the band was a Velvet Underground CD Nikolai Fraiture's brother gave Casablancas for Christmas in high school.

Karen O to Hot Press (Stuart Clark, 13 October 2006), naming Sonic Youth when asked which of her heroes she had met: "I tried so hard to be cool the first time we were introduced but no, I dorked out completely! How can you not when they’re the godfathers and godmother of experimental music?"
Max Bassin to Still Listening Magazine: "I was a big Strokes fan when I was in middle school and high school."

Peter Hook to NME (as told to Andrew Trendell, 6 May 2020): "Kraftwerk were such a huge influence on us, both musically and stylistically. Ian was so in awe of the way that they dressed and the way they acted as well as their music."

Steven Severin to The Guardian (2005): "we, perversely, saw ourselves as taking on the baton of glamorous art rock - Bowie and Roxy Music - while incorporating a love for Can, Kraftwerk and Neu."

The Quietus reported Thurston Moore speaking at Liverpool Sound City (interviewed by Dave Haslam) about "the early influence Moore took from British bands, mentioning Wire, The Pop Group, The Raincoats and The Slits".

Howard of The Birthday Party. We followed The Birthday Party all over and it's because of them that we sent a demo to 4AD."

Lou Barlow to Jason Gross in Perfect Sound Forever (January 1997): "There was stuff like the Birthday Party, Scratch Acid and Sonic Youth." Of Dinosaur Jr., he said they were "really influenced by Neil Young and Black Sabbath".
Far Out Magazine, in "How the Grateful Dead soundtracked Karen O’s teenage years", states that Karen O has named the Birthday Party among her influences.
Rolling Stone, on writing Psychocandy: "we got seriously into the Velvets and the Stooges."

Jim Reid of The Jesus and Mary Chain, choosing New York Dolls's New York Dolls for The Quietus's Baker's Dozen: "They are typical of everything we as the Mary Chain are into, it just seems like they're the real deal."
Thurston Moore to the Los Angeles Times (1985): "We're more influenced by the Stooges, MC5 or the Velvet Underground than composers like John Cage or Harry Partch."
Johnny Marr to Spin (2012): "I got the first two Stooges albums immediately after I got Raw Power, and I know every note and word on them."

Morrissey was a fan of the New York Dolls as a teenager, ran their British fan club, and wrote a 1981 booklet about them; Johnny Marr, also a Dolls fan, was impressed enough by that book to knock on his door and propose forming a band.
Iggy Pop to Rolling Stone, reported by NME (January 2016): he first met Bowie after hearing that Bowie liked the Stooges, "something not a lot of people would admit at the time."

Dangerous Minds' piece on Johnny Thunders and the Replacements says the New York Dolls and the Heartbreakers "both groups influenced the Replacements", and adds that Paul Westerberg brought the Dolls' debut to the band's first rehearsal in late 1979.
Bernard Sumner to Rolling Stone (2015): "Our earliest influences were Bowie and Iggy Pop and Kraftwerk and songwriters like Neil Young before that."

Robert Smith, quoted in NME's '27 Geeky Facts About The Cure' (5 Nov 2014), on playing guitar for the Banshees in 1979: "It was so different to what we were doing with The Cure. Far Out Magazine, relaying Nick Cave's 2013 interview with the German magazine Spex, quotes him: "David Bowie's not merely a performer... He was part of our childhood. In my eyes, Bowie stands for a certain kind of immortality," and calls Cave "a massive admirer of David Bowie and his artistry."

Bill Prince, "New 2 U: Cocteau Twins," Sounds (11 Sept 1982), describing the band as "mixing strong Siouxsie and the Banshees and Joy Division influences" -- a contemporary reviewer's reading rather than the band's own account.

Emma Anderson, FLOOD: "I was all about post-punk. I liked the Cocteau Twins and Siouxsie and the Banshees."

Ian Watson's sleeve notes to Slowdive's Souvlaki reissue: Brian Eno's fans in the band were Neil Halstead, "a big fan," and Christian Savill, who had a "special affinity" with Eno's Apollo; they sent him CDs and asked him to produce the next record. Eno declined to produce but collaborated on "Sing" and "Here She Comes."
Tim Hecker, RBMA lecture: "I was faking driver's license IDs so I could get into clubs to see bands like Ride or My Bloody Valentine play," describing his teenage years in Vancouver.

Tim Hecker, Red Bull Music Academy lecture: "I was faking driver's license IDs so I could get into clubs to see bands like Ride or My Bloody Valentine play. In Vancouver, that was like a huge thing if one of those bands came through town."
NPR's Lars Gotrich (2023), on Stars of the Lid: "Stars of the Lid started in Austin, Texas, in 1993. Brian McBride and Adam Wiltzie both loved Brian Eno."
James Murphy to John Doran, Noisey/VICE (12 Oct 2017): "The Fall are part of my DNA, arguably as much as David Bowie."
GRAMMY.com: "Their influences — ESG, Loose Joints, David Bowie, Talking Heads, CAN, Daft Punk, Kraftwerk — were spiritually present but seamlessly mixed in."
GRAMMY.com: "Their influences — ESG, Loose Joints, David Bowie, Talking Heads, CAN, Daft Punk, Kraftwerk — were spiritually present but seamlessly mixed in."
James Murphy to Time Out Abu Dhabi: "I like stuff from my childhood, early OMD or Bronski Beat or The Smiths, which was the kind of music you loved in your room..."

Hi-Fi News (Mike Barnes, Rock, June 2026): Hot Chip's "influences included Abba, Prince, OMD and Roxy Music."

Ben Gibbard on the Life of the Record podcast episode "The Making of Give Up" (Dan Nordheim, 2023): "so much like electronic pop music was stuff that we grew up on and we loved and that, you know, I grew up a huge Depeche Mode fan, a huge Kraftwerk fan, you know, a huge fan of the Pet Shop Boys and Erasure and all that kind of stuff, New Order."

Ben Gibbard to The Ringer (2023): "We were in the right place at the right time to resurrect the craftsmanship of that early '80s electronic music via Orchestral Manoeuvres in the Dark, Depeche Mode, or the Human League."

Ben Gibbard to The Ringer (2023), on Give Up: "We were in the right place at the right time to resurrect the craftsmanship of that early ’80s electronic music via Orchestral Manoeuvres in the Dark, Depeche Mode, or the Human League."

Dan Snaith to XLR8R ("Rewind: Caribou," Sept 30, 2014), on his first Manitoba album Start Breaking My Heart (2001): "In some ways, it was very much influenced by what Kieran was doing, Boards of Canada, and those kind of things, but also sampling off a lot of old records and things like that."

Dan Snaith of Caribou, in Pitchfork's 5-10-15-20 (2014), on his years around 20, when he was "constantly making and recording electronic music": "I was also listening to Tortoise, Stereolab, Boards of Canada, Aphex Twin, and Spiritualized—stuff on the fringes. I was interested in music that deconstructed the rules."

!!! to Stereogum's Turntable Interview, asked whether Depeche Mode and OMD influenced them: "things creep in here and there... some old depeche mode idea from a song u haven't listened to in years will creep in there... I want to always be as excited about new music as I was when depeche mode's albums would come out."

DMY (Felicity Martin, Feb 3, 2021), on SOPHIE's May 2020 interview with The Face: Depeche Mode's 'Just Can’t Get Enough' was "one of the inspirations behind the producer’s work", which SOPHIE called "an amazing achievement" that "established one part of the sound of the decade that followed".

Her brother and engineer Ben Long to MusicRadar: "Sophie's interest in Autechre came a little bit later... It was very much Draft 7.30 or Untilted onwards, mid-'00s to now, that was really the Autechre discography that she loved."

A.G. Cook, Line of Best Fit (2024, around Britpop): "I actually see her fingerprints as much on 'Silver Thread Golden Needle' and a lot of the instrumental tracks as I do on something like 'Without.'"
Charli XCX, accepting Best Dance Act at the 2025 BRIT Awards (reported by PinkNews): "And of course, someone who none of us would be up here without, SOPHIE."

Charli XCX at the 2025 BRIT Awards (reported by Crack Magazine): she thanked the "legends in the field" who inspired or shaped her music: "Shout out to Justice, Daft Punk, Sebastian, Honey Dijon, Robyn, Arca, M.I.A., Autechre, Aphex Twin."

Arca to GRAMMY.com (Jennifer Velez, 2021), on her older brother's records: "I think his musical tastes left a big influence on me. He had a lot of Aphex Twin, Squarepusher." The FADER's "Cover Story: Arca Finds Xen" (Emilie Friedlander, 2014) also describes her teenage Nuuro songs as "glitchy, Aphex Twin-inspired beat compositions."

Arca to GRAMMY.com (Jennifer Velez, 2021): "I have a brother seven years older, and I would often borrow his music... I think his musical tastes left a big influence on me. He had a lot of Aphex Twin, Squarepusher."

The FADER (Emilie Friedlander, "Cover Story: Arca Finds Xen", 2014) reports that, aided partly by an older brother's CD collection, Arca went through "a series of musical obsessions typical of kids growing up in the '90s—Aaliyah, Autechre, Nine Inch Nails, Marilyn Manson."

Ian Cohen, Stereogum, introducing a Q&A on Frailty: the songs are "rooted just enough in familiar formats - the saturated, EDM-adjacent ultrapop of Porter Robinson; SoundCloud rap's glitchy, bitcrushed production; the cleansing catharsis of emo."

Robinson, beside Ninajirachi on triple j's Breakfast with Abby and Tyrone (2026), on what he took from her into his own studio: her way with lyrics -- "just kind of like come up with stuff and not overthink it and go for it and sell it really. And I've been trying to carry that with me in the studio" -- and her "glitch generation" technique of recording an hour of crazy sound, which he has been using "so much" and which "led to so many breakthroughs."

Ninajirachi to MusicTech: "I've been a fan all the way through, and love everything he does," she says of Porter Robinson, whose logo is tattooed on her wrist; "It was very much the emotion I was drawn to [early on]... Or the contrast of the emotion and gorgeous chord progressions with the really, like, disgusting sound design."
MusicTech calls SOPHIE another of Ninajirachi's "musical heroes", invoked to show how SOPHIE "manipulated technology to bold and thrilling effect."
FLOOD Magazine's softscars interview (2023) says yeule finds inspiration in Aphex Twin and Suzanne Ciani: "They're not doing music by the book... they're doing it by the feeling."
yeule to DIY (Sept 2023), on the music they grew up on: "Oh we should totally do some Pixies shit, or Smashing Pumpkins!"
yeule to DIY (Sept 2023): "We have so many references from the '90s and '00s, like Radiohead, My Chemical Romance..."

FADER (2018, on Virtual Self): described trying to recreate "what electronic music sounded like when I was 12 years old, just typing the word 'techno' into Limewire and downloading horribly mislabeled songs by Aphex Twin and other artists."

Alexis Petridis, The Guardian (18 Oct 2021): Faust's "list of their admirers would include everyone from Stereolab to Simple Minds... to Radiohead, who paid homage with the title of 2007's Faust Arp."
Vice argued that Faust was "undoubtedly the muse unto which Sonic Youth owes royalties."

Wikipedia's Faust page lists the band as "cited as an influence by Radiohead, Swell Maps, Throbbing Gristle, Cabaret Voltaire, Stereolab, Simple Minds, Sonic Youth, Mark E. Smith, Nurse with Wound and Madlib."

Far Out Magazine reports that Robert Smith, listing five songs that changed his life for Richard Kingsmill on Triple J, named Nick Drake's "Time Has Told Me" and called Drake "everything I would aspire to in… understated mood songwriting and singing".

Far Out Magazine reports that Robert Smith, in his Triple J five-songs appearance with Richard Kingsmill, named the Sex Pistols' "Anarchy In The UK" as "the last time something really major happened to me and changed me".

Robert Smith to Rolling Stone (2004), as quoted by Far Out Magazine: "When I first saw The Stranglers, I thought, 'This is it.'" Then he "saw the Buzzcocks the following week, and I thought, 'This is definitely it.'"
Wikipedia's Nick Drake article reports that his producer Joe Boyd listed Bert Jansch among Drake's influences.

Uncut (June 2015 issue) reports that the first summer in Eugene Lowell Brams introduced Sufjan Stevens and his siblings to Nick Drake, among others; Stevens says "It was as if he had opened up a Pandora’s Box, and we were so thrilled."

Adrianne Lenker to The Ringer (2019): "I really admire Joni Mitchell, Neil Young, Leonard Cohen -- how they have such a breadth of material throughout the years, into old age." She is describing a career approach rather than a sound: "They seemed to follow their own thread of curiosity and creativity, even through some weird phases when people were like, 'I don't know what they're doing.'"

Wikipedia's Nick Drake article: as a teenager Drake learned songs by Bob Dylan on guitar, "having been particularly affected by Dylan's 'A Hard Rain's a-Gonna Fall'."
Nick Cave in the Red Hand Files, on his ten "hiding songs" ("They are the essential pillars that hold up the structure of my artistic world"): Leonard Cohen's "Avalanche" is on the list.
NTS describes Oklou's mix "choke soundscape" (2025) as "a dreamy soundscape of influences and sonic inspirations behind her debut album"; it includes Vashti Bunyan.
Joanna Newsom told The Believer that Devendra Banhart introduced her to Vashti Bunyan's music, an English singer from the sixties whose songwriting style she loves.
Vashti Bunyan, in Pitchfork's 5-10-15-20 (2014): "It also made me want to be a wandering singer myself."
Conor Oberst, on his own list of influences for Pitchfork (2020): "I think everybody is a combination of their influences, but Townes is the deep, dark part that I carry around."
Encyclopedia.com writes that Townes Van Zandt took up guitar at fifteen after being drawn in by blues records and early Bob Dylan, and FolkWorld has cited Dylan as a major influence on him.

Björk, on her official website (quoted by Far Out Magazine): "I was around fourteen, fifteen and I knew it by heart (still do, every instrument, every noise, every word)." The record was Joni Mitchell's Don Juan's Reckless Daughter.
Billboard (2020), on what Phoebe Bridgers geeked out on while making Punisher: bluegrass "along with Bright Eyes' I'm Wide Awake, It's Morning, influenced 'Graceland Too.'"

Johnny Marr to MusicRadar (2023), on who he named as his guitar influences in the early Smiths days: "when I had to really nail it down it was Nile Rodgers, Bert Jansch and James Williamson from The Stooges."

Joanna Newsom to Roy Harper in BOMB (2011): "There must have been a solid two years in particular when I didn't listen to anything except Roy Harper. So of course you have influenced the way I write, especially in terms of how those expansive song lengths can be navigated and structured, and pushed and pulled between instrumentation and leanness."

Uncut reports that Robin Pecknold, in a note written for journalists, listed Roy Harper among the musical influences at play on Helplessness Blues, and that Pecknold has acknowledged Harper's influence in the layered vocals at the start of "The Plains/Bitter Dancer".
In the same Believer interview, Joanna Newsom said she loves Karen Dalton, a sixties singer who ran with Fred Neil and Bob Dylan and had a beautiful voice.
Nick Cave in the Red Hand Files, on his ten "hiding songs" ("They are the essential pillars that hold up the structure of my artistic world"): Karen Dalton's "Katie Cruel" is on the list.

Mike Sandison to Pitchfork: "In the late-80s the three bands that were a huge influence on us were Front 242 to some extent, and-- to a large extent-- Nitzer Ebb and the Cocteau Twins." Marcus Eoin adds that they are "such huge fans of theirs."

Jonathan Bernstein reports in Rolling Stone (24 Sept 2020) that Kurt Vile began listening to John Prine in his early twenties after a fan told him he sounded like him, spending "one cool summer" on Prine's greatest hits; Vile says "The heartbreakers hit you first, but from then on out it got deeper all the time."

Rolling Stone (2020) on Fleet Foxes' "Sunblind": "the stunning litany of thanks for musicians gone before their time," reciting the names of Judee Sill, John Prine, Elliott Smith, Silver Jews' David Berman and more, "in a cosmic scroll of appreciation."

Uncut (June 2015 issue) reports that the first summer in Eugene Lowell Brams introduced Sufjan Stevens and his siblings to Bob Dylan, among others; Stevens says "It was as if he had opened up a Pandora’s Box, and we were so thrilled."
Kurt Vile to The Line of Best Fit (February 2011), on moving back to Philadelphia in 2003 and starting his first band, the Violators: "I was obsessed with Bob Dylan at the time."

The Missoula Independent reported that Robin Pecknold said he grew up listening to his parents' records, which included the Beach Boys, the Beatles, Simon and Garfunkel, the Band, Joni Mitchell, Bob Dylan and Crosby, Stills and Nash.

Elliott Smith in an NME webchat (2000), as reported by Far Out: "My father taught me to play 'Don't Think Twice, It's All Right'... I love Dylan's lyrics, but more than that, I love the fact that he loves writing lyrics."
No Depression wrote that Jeff Buckley "highly revered the poetry of Bob Dylan" and covered several Dylan songs, including "Mama You've Been on My Mind" and "Just Like a Woman."

Kurt Vile to Jayson Greene, The Village Voice, on Neil Young's "On the Beach": "I can't say I wasn't influenced by that, because it would be a total lie. But there's this guitar solo, and at the very end he bends a high note, and plays the same note on the neighboring string -- that sustained note changed my life."

Rolling Stone's Fleet Foxes profile quotes bandmate Skyler Skjelset on he and Robin Pecknold at school: "We'd sit around and blast Neil Young and Bob Dylan -- and the teacher would always squeeze in some ELO and Yes."
Providence Phoenix (1999) reports that Mark Kozelek says he had never heard of Leonard Cohen or Nick Drake as a young man, but admits to Neil Young.

Mac DeMarco to Patrick Hosken (MTV News interview, early 2023, quoted in Hosken's Weekly Neil newsletter, Sept 4, 2024): "I go back to Harvest more often than his other records just because I'm intrigued by the way it sounds."

Justin Vernon to Rolling Stone (2011): "I always had a dream to be that sort of student of Neil Young, one of those people who can sit down and write a song and have it be this full statement and sound good."

Guitar.com's interview with Phoebe Bridgers on Punisher (2020): "Phoebe cites everything from Billie Eilish ('her production is so cool') to Guided By Voices, Caroline Polachek, Mitski, and Big Thief as influences on Punisher."

Benjamin Nugent's biography Elliott Smith and the Big Nothing (2009), quoted on Wikipedia's Fugazi page, recounts a friend recalling Smith becoming "really super-obsessed" with Built to Spill and Fugazi, and admiring Ian MacKaye intensely.

Clairo, in her notes for her Apple Music Influences playlist of the songs she listened to most while making Sling (2021), on Elliott Smith's "I Didn't Understand": "Easily the most heartbreaking song I have ever heard. Vocal stacks became all the more important to me because of how emotional it can really be on its own."
Lindsey Jordan to Gothamist (7 June 2018), on seeing Fiona Apple live: "once I really submerged myself into her discography, I was changed."

Thom Yorke, in an excerpt from Jason Thomas Gordon's The Singers Talk (via Consequence, 2023): "When we were doing the second record [The Bends], I went to see Jeff Buckley before he died... that was one of those, 'It's OK to do that?' And it reminded me of this vulnerable part of me that I was choosing to hide."

Far Out reported, citing Mitski's New Yorker interview, that the revelation that music could diverge from mainstream pop came in the form of Jeff Buckley, who introduced her to a different form of songwriting.
Kory Grow reports in Rolling Stone (Feb 2015, '10 New Artists You Need to Know') that Mitski draws influence from Björk, among others, "because they all do what the fuck they want, and do it well."

Guitar.com's interview with Phoebe Bridgers on Punisher (2020): "Phoebe cites everything from Billie Eilish ('her production is so cool') to Guided By Voices, Caroline Polachek, Mitski, and Big Thief as influences on Punisher."

Sharon Van Etten to Interview magazine, asked by Molly Ringwald about her musical influences: "Scott Walker, Cocteau Twins, Rowland Stuart Howard, Joy Division, Roy Orbison and Celine Dion. Very melodic and orchestral, but also percussive and angsty and intense."

Sharon Van Etten to Jaan Uhelszki, CREEM (June 2025), asked how fans of her old records are reacting to the "goth" album: "I know people say how much different this sounds, but I've been listening to the Cure, Duran Duran, Joy Division, and Portishead since I was a teenager. It was a natural progression in a lot of ways, and it's who I am."

Sharon Van Etten, in Jagjaguwar's press bio for Remind Me Tomorrow (2019), on her trial session with producer John Congleton: "I gave him Suicide, Portishead, and Nick Cave’s Skeleton Tree as references and he got excited."

Weyes Blood (Natalie Mering) to The Quietus Baker's Dozen: "I think it was just being a fan of The Velvet Underground and wanting to check out his solo music. I stayed with it because I felt like he had a similar thing that I had: a keen interest in classical music."

Natalie Mering (Weyes Blood), choosing Can's Monster Movie for The Quietus's Baker's Dozen: "Can's Monster Movie was the first super weird record that I became obsessed with... It was the beginning of my foray into more experimental music."
Natalie Mering (Weyes Blood), choosing Cocteau Twins's Treasure for The Quietus's Baker's Dozen: "I feel like she gave me confidence to not have to always make sense"

Ethel Cain told The FADER in May 2022 that while making the record she was listening to slowcore and midwest emo acts like Title Fight and American Football, along with "female singers that are very lazy like Mazzy Star"; Nylon listed Mazzy Star's psychedelic melancholy among the album's ingredients that September.

Lindsey Jordan named Liz Phair in the same 2016 9:30 Club interview in which she named Grouper, Broadcast, Joni Mitchell, Psychic TV and Beat Happening as artists she was listening to while writing Habit.

Lindsey Jordan to Fender's Under the Influence series, on My Bloody Valentine's Bilinda Butcher: "She's a huge part of the band that created shoegaze... she's this huge figure in my songwriting and my life."

Lindsey Jordan said in a 2016 interview at the 9:30 Club, posted to Tumblr, that while writing Habit she was listening to a lot of Grouper, Broadcast, Joni Mitchell, Psychic TV, Beat Happening and Liz Phair, adding that not all of them influenced the album stylistically but she had learned from their songwriting, which she called articulate and inspirational.
The same 2016 9:30 Club interview names Broadcast alongside Grouper, Joni Mitchell, Psychic TV, Beat Happening and Liz Phair as artists Lindsey Jordan was listening to while writing Habit.

Michelle Zauner to Pitchfork, on making her third album Jubilee: "I was thinking about what musicians with long careers do with their third albums," pointing to Björk's Homogenic and Wilco's Summerteeth.
Michelle Zauner told CBC's Q that seeing Karen O, a fellow half-Korean woman, on stage was a big reason she felt the courage to start playing music herself.

Clairo to Far Out: "I'd say my musical influences are a mixture between my mom and dad's musical taste. My dad introduced me to soul music like Al Green, Brenton Wood, Billy Paul, etc. My mom introduced me to alternative music like Cocteau Twins, Trashcan Sinatras, The The, Public Image Ltd, etc. I would say that I fall somewhere in between."
CalArts blog (15 Oct 2015) on Julia Holter's VoiceArts Forum talk there (28 Sept 2015): the forum let her cover her varied musical influences, which include Cocteau Twins' "Fluffy Tufts".

Liz Phair on the inspiration for Soberish, in a statement reported by Rolling Stone Australia: "my art school years spent listening to Art Rock and New Wave music non-stop on my Walkman... Talking Heads, Velvet Underground, Laurie Anderson, and the Cars. The city came alive for me as a young person, the bands in my headphones lending me the courage to explore."
Liz Phair, in Pitchfork's 5-10-15-20 (2023): "It was my gateway drug into alternative."
Chan Marshall, CityBeat: "I think the Velvet Underground in general was a huge influence on me."
Chan Marshall to Jeff Niesel, CityBeat/Cleveland Scene (21 April 2022), on seeing Paul Westerberg throw his guitar off and run away after "Answering Machine": "It impacted me so much."

Chan Marshall to Jeff Niesel, CityBeat/Cleveland Scene (21 April 2022), on Nico: "Nico broke the mold by becoming a female icon. She was so broken. That European classical way of singing that I wanna say is very Catholic is very influential."
Wikipedia's Cat Power article: "When she was 13, she listened to the Smiths, the Cure and Siouxsie and the Banshees."

Wikipedia's Phil Elverum article says: "His musical influences include Eric's Trip, Will Oldham, Björk, Nirvana, Popol Vuh, Sunn O))))), Angelo Badalamenti, Tori Amos, The Cranberries, Sinéad O'Connor, Red House Painters, Sonic Youth, This Mortal Coil and Stereolab."
Alan Sparhawk to Andrea Swensson, The Current Rewind: Low: 25 Years In (7 Aug 2019): "Some of the bands we were inspired by—Spacemen 3, Joy Division, the Cure, Velvet Underground."
Alan Sparhawk of Low, choosing The Cure's Faith for The Quietus's Baker's Dozen: "It was definitely an early subconscious template for whatever Low was when we started."

Alan Sparhawk to Vice (Rank Your Records): "I remember hearing Codeine early on too and thinking, 'Wow, these guys are going way extreme with things that we're just barely touching.' I was pretty in awe of them. I remember having to force myself to not listen to Codeine and Red House Painters sometimes when I was writing, because I'd find myself falling too easily into their mannerisms and phrasings."
Have a Nice Life's own MySpace profile (2008) lists their influences as "My Bloody Valentine, Joy Division, New Order, Earth, Sunn, Xasthur, Lurker of Chalice, Nine Inch Nails" and others.
Have a Nice Life's own MySpace profile (2008) lists their influences as "My Bloody Valentine, Joy Division, New Order, Earth, Sunn, Xasthur, Lurker of Chalice, Nine Inch Nails" and others.

Kurt Vile to Rolling Stone (2021), as quoted by PhillyVoice: "Lou Reed/the Velvet Underground were probably my earliest classic rock influence... It just has an effect on you that you can't even necessarily detect at the moment."
Kurt Vile, in Pitchfork's 5-10-15-20 (2009): "Around '93, the radio started playing 'Loser' by Beck and 'Cut Your Hair' by Pavement, and then I got way into Pavement."

Kurt Vile to the Las Vegas Sun (30 Sept 2010), on his favourite Matador records: "I really love that I Can Feel the Heart Beating as One Yo La Tengo record a lot," adding "I'm just basically looking back to my teens."
RUSSH (Jasmine Pirovic, 9 March 2023) reports that in high school Kurt Vile's idols were bands like Pavement, Dinosaur Jr. and Sonic Youth.

Mac DeMarco, in a Guardian conversation reported by Far Out Magazine, singled out the Smiths' "Ask" as the song that made him "feel different at school": "At high school, people generally liked the same music I did, but when I started getting into the Smiths, everybody was like: 'Dude, why are you listening to this crap?'"

Stevie Chick, in his "A History of Modern Music: Indie" series: Ian MacKaye first met Bad Brains at a Cramps gig in DC in January 1979, forming Teen Idles after seeing them play, and later said "watching Bad Brains work was inspirational. . . They were the fastest, greatest band in the world."

Ian MacKaye to Rebel Noise (2009): "I always have to credit reading a Black Flag interview in Damage magazine from San Francisco in probably 1980 or '81. I think Dukowski the bass player said he'd rather work a day job for the rest of his life than ever become dependent on his music. And I thought, "That resonates with me in a hell of a way!""

The Wall Street Journal (2014), Marc Myers's piece on Interpol guitarist Daniel Kessler's five formative albums, runs under the subhead: "From Fugazi to PJ Harvey, the albums that helped give the guitarist an edge".
Wikipedia's Jeremiah Green article, citing a Modern Drummer interview (November 2015), says the Modest Mouse drummer named Fugazi as his biggest influence for starting a band.

Graham Coxon to Uncut (2017), on the mid-1990s: "Jo from Huggy Bear got me into things like Pavement and Slint and a lot of other small-label punk groups from the States – Universal Order Of Armageddon, Rites Of Spring, Fugazi. They used the guitar in an incredible way; making quite restrained noisy music, which I'd never heard English bands doing."
Uncut (2013) reported that when Justin Vernon started developing his own tastes he was attracted to the energy of Primus and Fugazi; he called Ian MacKaye "my fucking hero."
Eric Grubbs, Post: A Look at the Influence of Post-Hardcore 1985-2007 (2008), p.72: early influences "included Dischord Records bands like Rites of Spring... and Fugazi."
