edges.citation: Steve Holmes to TIDAL, "5 Albums That Changed My Life" (Ryan Pinkard, 21 October 2016), on Fugazi's Repeater: "But Fugazi was a game changer. I'd never heard anything like this." Fugazi led him into the Dischord catalogue: "It's impossible to overstate the influence of Dischord Records and the DIY ethic on me and our group of friends."
Mike Kinsella to Rolling Stone, in a story on American Football: "Cap'n Jazz had that sort of Dischord, Fugazi influence."

Jim Ward of At the Drive-In and Sparta, choosing a Fugazi record for Spin's "5 Albums I Can't Live Without" (2026): "Fugazi is my coming-of-age moment... So much of who I am as an artist was learned in this school—DIY and the ethics of our community."

Rolling Stone (2020), on Robin Pecknold: Elliott Smith is a "hugely, hugely formative" artist for him, who remembers going to the fansite sweetadeline.net in the early 2000s to look up guitar tabs.

Ethel Cain to The FADER (May 2022), on the change that made her Ethel Cain: "I was no longer listening to crazy heavy synth electronic music; I was listening to Nicole Dollanganger and Grouper and Slowdive and Def Leppard..."
Natalie Mering has said Joni Mitchell's Court and Spark played throughout her childhood, with her mother obsessed with Mitchell's music.

Alan Sparhawk to Andrea Swensson, The Current (2019), on how Low began: "There was some discussion at the beginning of stuff we were into... 'This really simple, drawn-out music is kind of cool. I wonder if we could bring that into a pop or band element?' We were looking at postmodern stuff too—La Monte Young. I guess you'd call Brian Eno kind of postmodern."

Sharon Van Etten to Jaan Uhelszki, CREEM (June 2025), asked how fans of her old records are reacting to the "goth" album: "I know people say how much different this sounds, but I've been listening to the Cure, Duran Duran, Joy Division, and Portishead since I was a teenager. It was a natural progression in a lot of ways, and it's who I am."

Robin Pecknold, in a letter (2011): "As a huge fan of hers, I was completely honored and flattered that she'd want me to open her shows, and I felt like I needed some new songs that I could play alone." Asked what was in regular rotation while recording Helplessness Blues, he named "Nic Jones, Beach House, Roy Harper, Dungen, Joanna Newsom, West Coast Pop Art Experimental Band."

Rolling Stone (2020) on Fleet Foxes' "Sunblind": "the stunning litany of thanks for musicians gone before their time," reciting the names of Judee Sill, John Prine, Elliott Smith, Silver Jews' David Berman and more, "in a cosmic scroll of appreciation."

Clairo, in her notes for her Apple Music Influences playlist of the songs she listened to most while making Sling (2021): "'Coyote' is one of the most important songs to me—for the weird guitar tunings, the unapologetic attitude, but mostly her words and metaphors. Genius, to say the least."

Julia Holter at CalArts' VoiceArts Forum (Sept 2015), as reported by the CalArts blog: "I love the way Ariel brings all these different voices together... Having tons of layers and voices is something that I love."

CalArts blog (15 Oct 2015) on Julia Holter's VoiceArts Forum talk there (28 Sept 2015): the forum let her cover her varied musical influences, which include Joni Mitchell's 1974 album Court and Spark.

Kory Grow reports in Rolling Stone (Feb 2015, '10 New Artists You Need to Know') that Mitski draws influence from J-pop singer Shiina Ringo, among others, "because they all do what the fuck they want, and do it well."
WRAL.com profile of Kurt Vile: as a teenager he "began studying indie rockers, especially Pavement, Beck, Sonic Youth and Dinosaur Jr."
Far Out reported that in the early days Mitski "looked up to innovators like St Vincent."
Lindsey Jordan named Joni Mitchell in the same 2016 9:30 Club interview in which she named Grouper, Broadcast and Liz Phair as artists she was listening to while writing Habit.

Far Out reported that Conor Oberst named the Replacements' "Here Comes a Regular" among eight songs that mattered to him, saying his late older brother Matty's friends "were fanatics about music" and "I'd sneak up to his room and steal his cassette tapes. All that came from him."

Have A Nice Life's own MySpace profile (archived 2008) lists its influences: My Bloody Valentine, Joy Division, New Order, Earth, Sunn, Xasthur, Lurker of Chalice, Nine Inch Nails, Swans, Sisters of Mercy, Kraftwerk and Nietzsche.

Have A Nice Life's own MySpace profile (archived 2008) lists its influences: My Bloody Valentine, Joy Division, New Order, Earth, Sunn, Xasthur, Lurker of Chalice, Nine Inch Nails, Swans, Sisters of Mercy, Kraftwerk and Nietzsche.

Tim Macuga to Steel for Brains ("The Big Gloom - A Conversation With Have a Nice Life", 21 February 2014), asked which bands from his youth had the biggest impact on him: "Yeah, the default music of my youth was the Dead Kennedys, Descendents, Op Iy."

Dev Hynes to Grammy.com (Aug 2025): "if I go back to when I was younger and the earliest things that informed me, it's the Smiths, Radiohead, New Order, Megadeth and Slipknot, Prefab Sprout." He also told AnOther (2025): "Some of my biggest lyrical references, like Morrissey, have a way with these really blunt sentences."

Natural Snow Buildings to OndaRock, asked about their influences: "La lista potrebbe andare avanti per pagine e pagine (da Kath Bloom e Loren Mazzacane Connors a Tarentel, Neil Young, Six Organs Of Admittance, Charalambides, Alice Coltrane, Stars Of The Lid, le colonne sonore, musica da ogni parte del mondo)" (the list of musicians who built their musical ethos; interview published in Italian).

Kurt Cobain in Melody Maker (1992), on Pod: "The main reason I like them is for their songs, for the way they structure them, which is totally unique, very atmospheric." He also said "I wish Kim was allowed to write more songs for the Pixies, because 'Gigantic' is the best Pixies song, and Kim wrote it." Kim Deal has separately said she believes Nirvana hired Steve Albini for In Utero because of Pod.

edges.citation: Kim Deal to PopMatters, asked "Is Neil one of your idols?": "Oh yeah. Absolutely. I was listening to a lot of Harvest last year, now that you mention it. Because my Volvo only has a cassette player, so I listened to that tape constantly. And I was listening to that a lot when I was writing Fate to Fatal." Cheryl Deal then teased her about an early version of "Pinnacle Hollow": "Oh, there you go. There's the Neil influence!"

Dean Ween to Berklee Online's Take Note podcast ("Dean Ween (Mickey Melchiondo) on the Guitarists That Shaped Him"), on the record collections he and Aaron Freeman grew up between: "Aaron's dad didn't have a lot of records either, but between the cool ones that I had and the cool ones he had, that's kind of what Ween is. He had everything from Nina Simone to the first two Velvet Underground records, to Richie Havens' Alarm Clock, to... I mean, everything, Beefheart... and so, those influences together..."
Sonic Boom (Peter Kember) to MOJO: "The big thing for me, that I took from The Velvet Underground into Spacemen 3, was the drone."
Sonic Boom to Forced Exposure (September 1988), on the band's one-chord, twenty-minute songs: "I think that's something we got from the Stooges, 'O.D. Catastrophe'."
Sonic Boom to Forced Exposure (September 1988): "We do a song called 'Suicide' which we dedicate to them every gig. It's kind of like Suicide and the Stooges crossed."
Andy Bell of Ride to Premier Guitar, on "bands that came a bit before us, like My Bloody Valentine, Spacemen 3, and Loop. They had a noise element that we found really cool."
Low, in The Current's "Low: 25 Years In" (2019): "Some of the bands we were inspired by—Spacemen 3, Joy Division, the Cure, Velvet Underground."
Phil Manzanera of Roxy Music on NPR's Weekend Edition (November 2022): "we loved The Velvet Underground. And, you know, they had very few chords in their songs. And it was about simplicity."
Dan Bejar in Pitchfork's 5-10-15-20: "I got lost in Avalon in an unhealthy way: the reverbs, the drum sounds, the percussion" -- and he wrote the songs on Kaputt shortly afterwards.
Martyn Ware of the Human League, choosing Roxy Music's debut for The Quietus's Baker's Dozen: "It changed my life... It was like an awakening."
Richard H. Kirk of Cabaret Voltaire, in The Quietus's Baker's Dozen: "Roxy Music were tremendously influential, not least of all on Cabaret Voltaire."
Steve Jones, in Spin's "5 Albums I Can't Live Without" (2025), on Roxy Music's For Your Pleasure: "it's one of them albums for me as a 15, 16 year old."

Viv Albertine, in her memoir as quoted by Far Out, on hearing Patti Smith's Horses: "If I can take a quarter or even an eighth of what she has and not give a shit about what people think of me, I'll be happy."

Viv Albertine, in her memoir as quoted by Bookforum, on seeing the Sex Pistols: "This is the first time I've seen a band and felt there are no barriers between me and them." She bought a guitar soon after.
Kathleen Hanna, choosing the Slits' Cut for The Quietus's Baker's Dozen: "Sonically they really changed my world and the freedom and the looseness... They taught me about production."
Allison Wolfe of Bratmobile in Pitchfork's 5-10-15-20: "The Slits have been hugely influential on me."
Mary Timony in Pitchfork's 5-10-15-20, on her teenage years: "I'd listen to the Slits' Cut on a cassette a lot in that car."

Stereogum (April 2023) reports that Suryakant Sawhney "cites the Velvet Underground and Neutral Milk Hotel as formative, not only for their sound, but for being emblematic of a distinctly American do-it-yourself ideal."
Rolling Stone India (April 2011) on Peter Cat Recording Co.: "Neutral Milk Hotel is a common favourite and one of the outfit's major influences."
Kate Bush, recalling hearing "Starman" on Radio Luxembourg as a teenager (quoted by Far Out): "Bowie's music became a part of my life."
Dev Hynes of Blood Orange, in The Quietus's Baker's Dozen: Hounds of Love is "probably the most influential album for me", and when he uses piano it is "essentially because of Kate Bush".
Michelle Zauner of Japanese Breakfast, in The Quietus's Baker's Dozen: Kate Bush's "Delius" was "a huge inspiration" for her song "Paprika".
Caroline Polachek to W Magazine (2022): Björk, Kate Bush and Fiona Apple "were my absolute heroes when I was a teenager."
Kevin Barnes of of Montreal, asked by DCist which artists influenced how he makes music, named a list including David Bowie, Prince and Kate Bush.
PJ Harvey to The Guardian (2001), as quoted by Far Out: "He has been a big influence on my work. I grew up on a diet of Dylan – my mum was a big fan."
Britt Daniel of Spoon in Pitchfork's 5-10-15-20: he was "definitely obsessed" with PJ Harvey around To Bring You My Love, and "I still reference To Bring You My Love when we make records."
Kurt Vile in The Quietus's Baker's Dozen: "PJ Harvey influences me all the time."
Annie Clark (St. Vincent), as quoted by Far Out, on first seeing PJ Harvey on MTV around 1998 and buying two of her records the next day; Is This Desire? became one of her favourite albums.
Seattle Met's "Points of Reference" for Tramp (2012): Sharon Van Etten listed PJ Harvey's Rid of Me, which producer Aaron Dessner kept referring to while they made the record.
David Bowie, on BBC Radio 1 in 1997, on Scott Walker: "I think he's probably been my idol since I was a kid."
Thom Yorke on Scott Walker's death (March 2019): he "was a huge influence on Radiohead and myself, showing me how i could use my voice and words."
Jarvis Cocker in Pitchfork's 5-10-15-20: "Leonard Cohen and Scott Walker are the two real touchstones in terms of people I've listened to consistently throughout my whole life."
Dan Bejar in Pitchfork's 5-10-15-20: in 2003 he was "wrestling with my intense love of Scott Walker" while making Your Blues.
Jamie Stewart of Xiu Xiu in The Quietus's Baker's Dozen: Scott Walker "is an idol of mine" and his trajectory "an incredible inspiration."

Kevin Drew of Broken Social Scene to Spacing Toronto, on hearing Dinosaur Jr.'s "The Wagon" at fourteen: "That was the first time I heard a new song that I immediately related to... That changed the course of my life."

Jockey Slut (2003) on Luke Jenner and Vito Roccoforte growing up in La Mesa, California: "In their school days they listened to a lot of college radio: The Smiths, Soft Cell, The Cure and Gary Numan."

Jockey Slut (2003) on Luke Jenner and Vito Roccoforte growing up in La Mesa, California: "In their school days they listened to a lot of college radio: The Smiths, Soft Cell, The Cure and Gary Numan."

Relix's profile of Angel Olsen: "From The Velvet Underground, Leonard Cohen and Neil Young to the ChiLites, Jackie DeShannon and Candi Staton" she draws from a wealth of influences.

Broward Palm Beach New Times: "'We're not metal, not hardcore, not noise,' Crow explains obliquely as he spouts off influences such as Captain Beefheart, the Shaggs, Black Flag, and Venom."
Kieran Hebden of Four Tet to the Independent Weekly: "I'm always coming back to the records by bands like Can and Kraftwerk. It's definitely a great era as music."
Kieran Hebden of Four Tet to the Independent Weekly: "I'm always coming back to the records by bands like Can and Kraftwerk. It's definitely a great era as music."
Do Make Say Think, picking Talk Talk's "New Grass" for AdHoc (December 2017): "this band and their two final records are SUPER influential to our band."
Steve Holmes of American Football, in TIDAL Magazine's "5 Albums That Changed My Life": "Wilco set me on a path to rediscover the guitar, standard tuning, and just great songwriting."
Noah Lennox (Panda Bear) of Animal Collective, in Red Bull Music Academy Daily's oral history of the band (2018): "That and Aphex Twin really changed the course of my musical life."

Jim Ward of At the Drive-In and Sparta, choosing the Clash's Combat Rock for Spin's "5 Albums I Can't Live Without" (2026): "This is the band that taught me about world influence; it is not just the music but the intent."
Jim Ward of At the Drive-In and Sparta, in Spin's "5 Albums I Can't Live Without" (2026): "I learned to play bass by playing along with the Pixies and Dead Kennedys."

Stuart Murdoch of Belle and Sebastian, in Pitchfork's 5-10-15-20 (2015), on sitting in on Camera Obscura's early rehearsals: "They were a real guide and made me think, 'We need to get back to playing simple music again.'"

Steve Albini, asked about his formative years in an interview with VW Music Rocks: "As a musician, I was formed by being embedded in the Punk scene... My favorite bands during that era include... bands that inspired me like... a bunch of overseas bands like the Birthday Party..."

Steve Albini, asked about his formative years in an interview with VW Music Rocks: "As a musician, I was formed by being embedded in the Punk scene... My favorite bands during that era include... bands that inspired me like... a bunch of overseas bands like the Birthday Party... Contortions..."

Cameron Picton of black midi, in Stereogum's Under the Influence: a neighbour who taught him guitar "showed me all this Bert Jansch stuff... I got really into it," and he still names Jansch as a guitarist he particularly likes.
Graham Coxon of Blur, asked in Uncut about the moment that changed everything in his early days: "Things like Robert Wyatt, Van der Graaf Generator and The Velvet Underground really excited me."

Brian Eno, on Joni Mitchell's Court and Spark in The Quietus's Baker's Dozen: "I remember buying this album when it came out in 1974 because I know it had a big impact on what I was working on at the time, which was Another Green World. When I heard this record I really thought that I've got to change what I'm doing."

Richard H. Kirk of Cabaret Voltaire, on David Bowie's Low in The Quietus's Baker's Dozen: "I was a Bowie fan from about 15. I went to see the Ziggy Stardust tour in Sheffield and was kind of blown away," and Bowie embracing electronic music "did Cabaret Voltaire and a lot of people like us a favour."

Chan Marshall (Cat Power), on Hüsker Dü's Metal Circus in The Quietus's Baker's Dozen, a cassette her sister gave her for her twelfth birthday: "I loved that fucking record, that tape, so much... All these impossible sounds were making sense."

Milo Aukerman of the Descendents, in Pitchfork's 5-10-15-20: "I started out with X, and then I graduated to the Germs, and then Black Flag. Those three bands are the holy trinity of L.A. punk rock to me."
Dan Bejar of Destroyer, in Pitchfork's 5-10-15-20: "At 15, I was deep in the clutches of the Jesus and Mary Chain. That was the first noisy thing I liked."
Ian McCulloch of Echo & the Bunnymen, on David Bowie's Hunky Dory in The Quietus's Baker's Dozen: "It was Bowie was who got me interested in music, then I got into the Velvets and Iggy."

Will Sergeant of Echo & the Bunnymen, on Television's Marquee Moon in The Quietus's Baker's Dozen: "I learnt all the wobbly guitar sounds you hear on the Bunnymen records from this. I've been living off that ever since, really."

Dazed (2018), reporting on Grimes: she calls Burial one of her "all-time favourite artists" and "cites the elusive London producer among artists she considers herself a descendent of (Aphex Twin and Animal Collective included)."
Alexis Taylor of Hot Chip, on Neil Young's On the Beach in The Quietus's Baker's Dozen: "Neil Young was the first songwriter whose songs I learned to play on the guitar."
Paul Banks of Interpol, in Pitchfork's 5-10-15-20, on Nirvana's Nevermind: "Nirvana helped me understand that music was what I wanted to do with my life."

Michelle Zauner of Japanese Breakfast, in The Quietus's Baker's Dozen: "My other big influence on [For Melancholy Brunettes (& Sad Women)] was Sufjan Stevens' Carrie & Lowell... That was a huge inspiration for me."

Liz Phair, in Pitchfork's 5-10-15-20, on the Human League's "Don't You Want Me": "it also became really formative for me, because it was the first time I had heard a woman clapping back in a song... Guyville wouldn't be Guyville without the Human League."

Alan Sparhawk of Low, on the Clash's Combat Rock in The Quietus's Baker's Dozen: "I remember learning the chords to that song on the guitar, and that was the big lightning bolt going on. It was like 'Wow, really, you can do this? I can do this?'"

Mary Timony, in Pitchfork's 5-10-15-20, on her first punk show in 1985, Rites of Spring and Beefeater: "That totally changed my life... my favorite band from that time was Rites of Spring, and it still is."

Mike Watt of the Minutemen, on the Stooges' Fun House in The Quietus's Baker's Dozen: "I had to learn bass from Fun House, Creedence and the brothers doing R&B... Fun House was a freak out moment for us."
Stuart Braithwaite of Mogwai, on David Bowie's Low in The Quietus's Baker's Dozen: "Bowie is one of the people who made me consider that I liked music. It was a really important, formative thing."

Kevin Shields of My Bloody Valentine, in Mixdown's Gear Talks: "Basically, we started out as a band that was really into The Birthday Party and Einstürzende Neubauten. Quite physical... quite aggressive."

Kevin Barnes of Of Montreal, asked by DCist (2015) which musicians have influenced the way he makes music: "Yeah, definitely David Bowie, Prince, Kate Bush, Iggy Pop, Lou Reed, John Lennon, Leonard Cohen, Ray Davies, Skip Spence, Patti Smith..."

Stephen Malkmus of Pavement, on the Dead Kennedys in the Guardian's Soundtrack of My Life (2013): "This album was a gateway towards sarcasm and questioning authority... I was listening to them in mid-late high school, 1981-82."
Mike Hadreas of Perfume Genius, on Björk in The Quietus's Baker's Dozen: "She was kind of my first true obsession. I had a Björk website where I just typed out all her lyrics."
Mark Webber of Pulp, on Big Star's Third in The Quietus's Baker's Dozen: "It was records like this that I aspired to make when I was young."
David Pajo of Slint, on Minor Threat's Out of Step in The Quietus's Baker's Dozen: "it was one of those life-altering LPs in that I was never the same afterwards."

Neil Halstead of Slowdive, on Talk Talk in The Quietus's Baker's Dozen: "This was a massive influence on Pygmalion. It's all about the way they used the space and how it slides into abstraction at points."

Lee Ranaldo of Sonic Youth, on Talking Heads in The Quietus's Baker's Dozen: "In the late 70s, I was moving to New York and I was inspired by all this stuff coming out of CBGB's, and Talking Heads was one of the hugest influences at that time."
J Spaceman of Spiritualized, on the Stooges' Raw Power in Pitchfork's 5-10-15-20: "my whole life premise and what I do is kind of built around that record."

Michael Gira of Swans, asked about influences in an interview with Young God Records: "particularly in the early days, I had a lot of influences... I listened to a wide variety of music then: The Stooges, Suicide, Throbbing Gristle, SPK, Cabaret Voltaire, Whitehouse, Brian Eno, Kraftwerk, No New York, Wire, Sex Pistols, Buzzcocks, Black Flag."

Michael Gira of Swans, asked about influences in an interview with Young God Records: "particularly in the early days, I had a lot of influences... I listened to a wide variety of music then: The Stooges, Suicide, Throbbing Gristle... Sex Pistols, Buzzcocks, Black Flag."

Michael Gira of Swans, asked about influences in an interview with Young God Records: "particularly in the early days, I had a lot of influences... I listened to a wide variety of music then: The Stooges, Suicide, Throbbing Gristle... Sex Pistols, Buzzcocks, Black Flag."

Brix Smith Start of the Fall, on Joy Division's Unknown Pleasures in The Quietus's Baker's Dozen: "I think this is the album that made me want to play bass. It made me sit up and say, 'I want to be in a band.'"

Matt Berninger of the National, on The Sound of Young America (Maximum Fun): "I've been a huge fan of people like Tom Waits and Leonard Cohen and The Smiths and Nick Cave... Neil Young and Bob Dylan, those kinds of guys. So the idea of actually trying to do that, to write good lyrics, was something really exciting to me."

Ben Gibbard of the Postal Service, to The Ringer (2023): "We were in the right place at the right time to resurrect the craftsmanship of that early '80s electronic music via Orchestral Manoeuvres in the Dark, Depeche Mode, or the Human League."
The Radio Dept.'s own website (2007), under "Influences," says what the band listens to instead of Slowdive and the Jesus and Mary Chain, and the list includes Nick Drake.

Johnny Marr of the Smiths, on Wire's 154 in The Quietus's Baker's Dozen: "As a young guitar player, discovering 154 showed me a world that was an alternative way of looking at the instrument. It has stuck with me all the way through my career."

Ian Brown of the Stone Roses, in the Guardian's Soundtrack of My Life (2010), on the Sex Pistols: "I was really into punk when I was about 14... We couldn't wait for the LP and when it came out it blew us away."

Justin Trosper of Unwound, asked about his influences in an interview on Scaruffi.com: "Greg Ginn (black flag), Sonic Youth, Greg Sage (wipers), Jimi Hendrix, David Lester (mecca normal), Helios Creed (chrome), Tom Verlaine (television), Toni Iommi (black sabbath) and more."
Katie Crutchfield of Waxahatchee, in Rolling Stone: "R.E.M. was a big influence. I saw R.E.M. on their last tour, in an arena... then I saw them and they just blew me away."

WRSU's profile of Xandy Chelmis of Wednesday: "Before he fell in love with Jason Molina and Jeff Tweedy, there were Neil Young LPs and Dr. Demento radio sets. His childhood favorites sparked a desire to play live."
Graham Lewis of Wire, on Neil Young in The Quietus's Baker's Dozen: "He's in Wire's minimalism, and you can see his influence go right through."

Jamie Stewart of Xiu Xiu, on the Cure in The Quietus's Baker's Dozen: "When I was in 10th grade, I listened to 'Kiss Me Kiss Me Kiss Me' every single night before I went to bed for an entire year," and the songs "get me on both an emotional and technical level."

American Football, in Tidal Magazine's "5 Albums That Changed My Life": "We never saw Rites of Spring, but their record mattered to us," after Fugazi led them back to Rites of Spring and the Dischord catalogue.

Jim Ward of At the Drive-In and Sparta, choosing Radiohead's OK Computer for Spin's "5 Albums I Can't Live Without" (2026): "If Joe Strummer made me want to be a better man, Radiohead made me want to be a better musician."

Stuart Murdoch of Belle and Sebastian, choosing The Smiths' The Queen Is Dead for The Quietus's Baker's Dozen: hearing "Bigmouth Strikes Again", "I became a different person... it confirmed everything about what kind of person I wanted to be."
Steve Albini of Big Black, interviewed by VW Music Rocks: "As a musician, I was formed by being embedded in the Punk scene," naming Bad Brains among the bands that inspired him.

Kathleen Hanna of Bikini Kill, in Pitchfork's 5-10-15-20: she listened to Bratmobile's The Real Janelle a lot because it was produced much better than Bikini Kill's records: "The quality of sound was really influential for me."
Kazu Makino of Blonde Redhead, in Pitchfork's 5-10-15-20: seeing Lush and My Bloody Valentine in New York, "Oh my god, this is what I want to do. I want this noise."

Graham Coxon of Blur, in Uncut: in the mid-1990s Jo Johnson of Huggy Bear got him into Pavement and Slint, who "used the guitar in an incredible way; making quite restrained noisy music, which I'd never heard English bands doing."
Jesse Lacey of Brand New, asked to Drowned in Sound (2009) what influenced the new record: "We were listening to Superchunk, Archers Of Loaf, Polvo, Modest Mouse..."
Conor Oberst of Bright Eyes, in Pitchfork's 5-10-15-20, on his teenage years writing songs: "I got really into Elliott Smith around that same period... I absolutely fell for it."
Dan Snaith of Caribou, in XLR8R's Rewind (2014), on his first record: "it was very much influenced by what Kieran was doing, Boards of Canada, and those kind of things."
Dan Bejar of Destroyer, choosing Joni Mitchell's Court and Spark for The Quietus's Baker's Dozen: on Poison Season, "I had songs like those Court And Spark songs in mind."

Ian McCulloch of Echo & the Bunnymen, in The Quietus's Baker's Dozen: "Every rhythm guitar part I've ever played I've just nicked from Lou Reed... When I met the right people later in life I would use the Velvets model."
Will Sergeant of Echo & the Bunnymen, in The Quietus's Baker's Dozen: seeing Brian Eno with Roxy Music, "I thought, 'right, I can kinda do that!'... that's when I started getting into recording."

Jonathan Higgs of Everything Everything, choosing Nirvana for The Quietus's Baker's Dozen: hearing "Lithium" was "the most exciting thing I'd ever heard", and soon after, "I knew that all I had to do was pick up that bass and we had a band."
Damon Krukowski of Galaxie 500, in Pitchfork's 5-10-15-20 with Damon & Naomi: Power, Corruption & Lies "was the college record for us. We listened to it endlessly."
Dazed reported that Grimes counts Animal Collective, with Burial and Aphex Twin, among the artists she considers herself a descendant of.
Bob Mould of Hüsker Dü, in The Quietus's Baker's Dozen: after getting the first Ramones record for his 16th birthday, seeing four guys carrying their own PA: "I'd rather do that."

Michelle Zauner of Japanese Breakfast, in The Quietus's Baker's Dozen: "When I started playing guitar, it was important for me to learn how to do finger-picking style because of those Elliott Smith records."
Fender's profile of Kurt Vile states that his early home-recorded cassettes were influenced by the likes of Pavement and Beck.
Liz Phair, in Pitchfork's 5-10-15-20: Pavement's Slanted and Enchanted was on repeat on her Walkman as she made Exile in Guyville: "it was my war call."
Emma Anderson of Lush, in The Quietus's Baker's Dozen: Hüsker Dü "influenced my early songwriting... I loved the freneticness of their music, coupled with these brilliantly written, clever songs."
Mary Timony, in Pitchfork's 5-10-15-20, on a tape of The Velvet Underground she played for three weeks on a road trip: "That record changed the way I thought of music completely."

Stuart Braithwaite of Mogwai, in Pitchfork's 5-10-15-20, on when the band started: "We were interested in a lot of American rock bands like Sonic Youth and Slint, as well as 70s guitar bands like the Stooges and Television."
Stephen Morris of New Order, in The Quietus's Baker's Dozen: "As a drummer, Klaus Dinger was important to me: [he taught me] how to make one riff last a lifetime!"

Kevin Barnes of of Montreal, in Pitchfork's 5-10-15-20, on the Elephant 6 bands in Athens including Neutral Milk Hotel: "That's where I learned that DIY approach to music making... if these guys can do it, I can too."

Mike Hadreas of Perfume Genius, in Tidal Magazine's "5 Albums That Changed My Life": having never heard Talk Talk when people asked after his third album if they were an influence, he listened, "became really obsessed with them and now I really do count them as an influence."
Adrian Utley of Portishead, in The Quietus's Baker's Dozen: Neil Young's album "was massive when I was a kid. It has never left me... his life is an inspiration."
Mark Webber of Pulp, in Spin's "5 Albums I Can't Live Without" (2024): "I've tried to introduce some elements of Adrianne Lenker and Buck Meek's approach into my parts."
Andy Bell of Ride, in The Quietus's Baker's Dozen: at 13 he was getting into The Cure and The Smiths, and Seventeen Seconds "has stayed with me all this time."
Steve Jones of the Sex Pistols, in Spin's "5 Albums I Can't Live Without" (2025), on David Bowie's glam-era albums: "Very inspirational to me. Steered me in the direction."

Neil Halstead of Slowdive, in The Quietus's Baker's Dozen, on the post-ambient scene that fed Pygmalion: "for me it all came from hearing SAW 85-92 [Aphex Twin] and wanting to try something a bit different."
Lee Ranaldo of Sonic Youth, in The Quietus's Baker's Dozen, on Joni Mitchell: "I love her guitar playing and the tunings, and it's just constant inspiration for me."
Lee Ranaldo of Sonic Youth, in The Quietus's Baker's Dozen, on Pavement: "they made this music that inspired me almost more so than anybody else at the time."
Lee Ranaldo of Sonic Youth, in Pitchfork's 5-10-15-20, on the early-80s SST scene: "We were very energized by it... the Minutemen always represented something a little bit closer to my heart."

Britt Daniel of Spoon, in The Quietus's Baker's Dozen, on Wipers' Over the Edge: asked if that "heavy but still pop template" inspired Spoon, "I think so," and he covered its songs on a four-track to figure out how songs were put together.
Laetitia Sadier of Stereolab, in The Quietus's Baker's Dozen, on The Smiths, first heard as a French adolescent: "I think the real power that hit me was in this record; the urgency and the energy."
Michael Gira of Swans, in a Young God Records interview: in the early days he had "a lot of influences" and listened to a wide variety including Brian Eno and Kraftwerk.
Michael Gira of Swans, in a Young God Records interview: in the early days he had "a lot of influences" and listened to a wide variety including Cabaret Voltaire, Throbbing Gristle and Wire.

Michael Gira of Swans, in The Quietus's Baker's Dozen: "Drake was inspirational to me in thinking about the simplicity and about creating something that has genuine power and truth in it, with very simple means."
Lol Tolhurst of The Cure, in The Quietus's Baker's Dozen: "Joe Strummer started me on this path... I knew that if he could do that, then so can I."

Matt Berninger of The National, on Bullseye with Jesse Thorn: he was obsessed with lyric-heavy writers, "Neil Young and Bob Dylan, those kinds of guys. So the idea of actually trying to do that, to write good lyrics, was something really exciting to me."
The Radio Dept.'s own site (2007), in its "Influences" section, lists Broadcast among the bands they listen to.
Johnny Marr of The Smiths, in The Quietus's Baker's Dozen: "Buzzcocks influenced The Smiths massively in the way we approached our record sleeves and our choice of independent record company."
...And You Will Know Us by the Trail of Dead, in a Metropolis Japan interview: "At the time we were influenced by bands who we knew like Unwound and Karp, but also bands like Sonic Youth."

Xandy Chelmis of Wednesday, on WRSU, on his high-school listening: "I really loved The Shins, Grizzly Bear, Real Estate, Beach Fossils... those bands were definitely informing me pretty heavily at the time."

Karly Hartzman of Wednesday, to Chasing Sundays (2025): a childhood friend played her Sunny Day Real Estate, Cocteau Twins and My Bloody Valentine, and she thought "I get music, and I want my life to revolve around music."

Karen O of Yeah Yeah Yeahs, in the Guardian's Soundtrack of My Life, on Neutral Milk Hotel's Jeff Mangum: "I can credit him for putting the idea in my head that I could sing too, as long as I sang my heart out."

Win Butler of Arcade Fire, in his Red Bull Music Academy lecture, recalling the poster the band made when looking for drummers: it listed "New Order, Debussy, Arvo Part, the Pixies", which he says is "pretty much what our band sounds like."
Jim Ward of At the Drive-In, in Spin's "5 Albums I Can't Live Without" (2026): "I learned to play bass by playing along with the Pixies and Dead Kennedys."

Stuart Murdoch of Belle and Sebastian, choosing The Fall's This Nation's Saving Grace for The Quietus's Baker's Dozen: "It had a great effect on me at the time... this crazy ranter, Mark E Smith, appealed to me deeply."
Steve Albini, asked about his formation as a musician, said he was "formed by being embedded in the Punk scene" and named the Minutemen among "local/regional bands that inspired me".
Henry Rollins, in Pitchfork's 5-10-15-20 (2019): "Alan Vega was a hero to me growing up because of the first Suicide record."
Kazu Makino of Blonde Redhead, in Pitchfork's 5-10-15-20 (2023), on opening for Unwound: "I never said it, but I felt like I was their student."
Graham Coxon of Blur, in Premier Guitar: "Yo La Tengo and Pavement were also great encouragement to do whatever I wanted when I had the space."
Brian Eno, choosing My Bloody Valentine's Glider for The Quietus's Baker's Dozen, said hearing singing buried in the noise "was a real liberation for me."
Steve Diggle of Buzzcocks, choosing David Bowie's Panic in Detroit for The Quietus's Baker's Dozen: "Bowie was an inspiration to [Buzzcocks] like The Beatles were."
Dan Snaith of Caribou, choosing Silver Apples' debut for The Quietus's Baker's Dozen: "People who know my albums from ten years ago will have heard me trying to rip off Silver Apples."
Chan Marshall (Cat Power), choosing Bob Dylan's Desire for The Quietus's Baker's Dozen, said she grew up with his records: "Loved Bob. Loved him. 'Tangled Up In Blue' was fucking watershed for me."
Milo Aukerman of the Descendents, in Pitchfork's 5-10-15-20 (2016): "Bad Brains had put out the 'Pay to Cum' single in 1980, and that had a huge effect on us."
Dan Bejar of Destroyer, in Pitchfork's 5-10-15-20 (2012): "When Slanted and Enchanted came out, everything changed." He bought an electric guitar and amp then.
Rick Froberg of Drive Like Jehu, interviewed by Vish Khanna in 2005: "I'm sure we aped Fugazi, who we were big fans of."

Ian McCulloch of Echo & the Bunnymen, choosing Leonard Cohen for The Quietus's Baker's Dozen: he saw Bird on the Wire at 14 and bought all his albums, and says of Cohen's way of turning lyrics on their head, "it's what I do a lot."
Tom Smith of Editors, in a Gigwise interview: "we build on the sound of the likes of Joy Division, Echo and the Bunnymen and The Chameleons."
Gary Numan, choosing Depeche Mode's Songs of Faith and Devotion for The Quietus's Baker's Dozen: "It's a massively important album and it helped to massively change my own direction."

Robert Pollard of Guided by Voices, choosing Wire's 154 for Spin's "The Records That Changed My Life" (2004): "When we started, we wanted to sound like a bunch of different bands... That was the Wire influence."

Bob Mould of Hüsker Dü, choosing Joy Division's Unknown Pleasures for The Quietus's Baker's Dozen: "This is it, this is what we're gonna do with music now... I take that lesson and I put it on my own stuff."

Michelle Zauner of Japanese Breakfast, choosing Joanna Newsom's Ys for The Quietus's Baker's Dozen: hearing Newsom's first record made her feel she could be a compelling singer with a weird voice, and Newsom's songwriting "sort of gave me the courage to be a singer."
Joanna Newsom, in The Believer, asked who her inspirations and influences are: "I love Donovan, Kate Bush, Leonard Cohen. Dylan, of course."

Alan Sparhawk of Low, in Vice's ranking of Low's albums: "I remember having to force myself to not listen to Codeine and Red House Painters sometimes when I was writing, because I'd find myself falling too easily into their mannerisms and phrasings."
Robert Del Naja of Massive Attack, in a Quietus interview about Heligoland: "PiL were a major influence on me with what they went for on Metal Box, and The Clash were really important as well."

Stuart Braithwaite of Mogwai, asked what he played as a budding guitarist: "The bands that I was really excited by were things like Jimi Hendrix and The Velvet Underground and quite simple stuff like The Cure and The Jesus and Mary Chain."

Stuart Braithwaite of Mogwai, in Pitchfork's 5-10-15-20 (2011), on the band's start: "We were interested in a lot of American rock bands like Sonic Youth and Slint, as well as 70s guitar bands like the Stooges and Television."

Kevin Barnes of of Montreal, in Pitchfork's 5-10-15-20 (2010), on seeing Neutral Milk Hotel and the Olivia Tremor Control play bigger shows: "I saw what was possible, like, if these guys can do it, I can too."
Mike Hadreas (Perfume Genius), choosing Patti Smith's Horses for The Quietus's Baker's Dozen: "I count the cover as an influence."
Geoff Barrow of Portishead, choosing Can's Ege Bamyasi for The Quietus's Baker's Dozen: "Can are my favourite and most inspirational band ever, I think."

Andy Bell of Ride, choosing Mazzy Star's She Hangs Brightly for The Quietus's Baker's Dozen: "I've taken on board a lot from David Roback's guitar playing... Roback and the other members of The Rain Parade were very influential on me."

Sharon Van Etten, in the Observer's Soundtrack of My Life (2015), on Low's Two-Step: "My friend Paul played me this when I was in college, and it just killed me... I tried to cover this at one of my early open-mic nights."

Neil Halstead of Slowdive, choosing Leonard Cohen's Songs of Love and Hate for The Quietus's Baker's Dozen: "That album really hit me and it made me aware of music that wasn't just a wall of guitars... it embedded itself in me."

Lee Ranaldo of Sonic Youth, choosing Leonard Cohen's Songs of Love and Hate for The Quietus's Baker's Dozen: "Cohen's another person I just constantly go back to for inspiration, especially these days as I'm writing more songs on my own."
Lee Ranaldo of Sonic Youth, in Pitchfork's 5-10-15-20 (2012), on Neil Young's After the Gold Rush: "There was a time when I could play almost every song on that record on my guitar."
Britt Daniel of Spoon, in NME's Soundtrack of My Life (2020): "The Violent Femmes were probably the biggest band for me in that burst of new freedom, I just completely related to their lyrics."

Michael Gira of Swans, asked about Swans' early sound: "particularly in the early days, I had a lot of influences... I listened to a wide variety of music then - The Stooges, Suicide, Throbbing Gristle..."
Michael Gira of Swans: "particularly in the early days, I had a lot of influences... I listened to a wide variety of music then - ... Wire, Sex Pistols, Buzzcocks, Black Flag."

Lol Tolhurst of The Cure, choosing Can's Tago Mago for The Quietus's Baker's Dozen, on Jaki Liebezeit's drumming: "there's this whole space inside of it that you can listen to and focus on with the push and pull. That's what I was always trying for."
Martyn Ware of the Human League, as reported by Post-Punk.co.uk from his talk at Walthamstow Trades Hall: Brian Eno specifically influenced his interest in making music.
Jimmy Tamborello of the Postal Service, in Life of the Record's notes on the album: "That song in particular was definitely Bjork. So yeah, her music definitely influenced the songs on the album."
On its own 2007 website, under the heading "Influences", The Radio Dept. listed the artists it listens to, among them Joy Division.
On its own 2007 website, under the heading "Influences", The Radio Dept. listed the artists it listens to, among them Neu!.
Johnny Marr of The Smiths, choosing Brian Eno's Taking Tiger Mountain for The Quietus's Baker's Dozen: "being a teenager during the 70s meant I never stopped being affected by Brian's music."
Justin Trosper of Unwound, asked about inspiration for Fake Train: "Yeah, VU and Sonic Youth are big influences."
Ezra Koenig of Vampire Weekend, in Pitchfork's 5-10-15-20 (2010), on the Walkmen's first album: "I was already really into the first album... it really struck a chord with me at that time."
Xandy Chelmis of Wednesday, on WRSU: "Fleet Foxes was a big one for me... those bands were definitely informing me pretty heavily at the time."
Jeff Tweedy of Wilco, in Pitchfork's 5-10-15-20 (2018), on the Minutemen: "They felt attainable... That was liberating for kids like me."
Jamie Stewart of Xiu Xiu, in the San Diego Reader, on Angel Guts: Red Classroom: "It is an homage to Suicide, Einstürzende Neubauten, Nico, and Kraftwerk."
James McNew of Yo La Tengo, in Pitchfork's 5-10-15-20 (2018): "At that point, Damaged by Black Flag had great sway over me and to this day it still does."

Tricky, writing in MOJO (July 2003, quoted by Kate Bush News) on how The Kick Inside changed his life: "I'd be an average musician, like everyone else, if it wasn't for her"; his "Strugglin'" was inspired by her "Breathing".
Tricky to The Skinny (2008, on Knowle West Boy): "Polly Harvey still inspires me, lyrically, and people like Rakim and Public Enemy."
John Darnielle to Magnet (June 2017, on Goths), recalling seeing the Cure in his mid-'80s goth days: "The Cure counts for all goths... they're so good, they transcend all that."
Harold Budd to Ceasefire Magazine (2012): "When it comes to the use of the studio, I learned everything from Eno."
George Clanton to Orlando Weekly (April 2024): "The first Mirror Kisses album -- that I've since erased from the Internet -- was me making what I thought was a Human League record."

Mike Sandison of Boards of Canada, asked about the folk in Geogaddi (interview with René Passet for Forcefield, reproduced on bocpages.org): "We love artists like Joni Mitchell and The Incredible Stringband. There's a sort of purity of sound that they have, and I guess we are striving for that ourselves."

Hirokazu Yamazaki of toe to Tone Glow (2024), on the American bands whose sound shaped his scene, Cap'n Jazz among them: "I listened to the music, but I had no idea how they played any of it or how their shows looked."
Will Sergeant in The Quietus's Baker's Dozen: by Ocean Rain (1984) "it was Scott Walker, Love, Jacques Brel; these were the main reasons we went to Paris."

Stephen McRobbie of the Pastels, choosing The Velvet Underground & Nico for his Quietus Baker's Dozen (2013): "This record was such a big influence on The Pastels, as was all The Velvet Underground's music."

Stephen McRobbie of the Pastels, choosing Kraftwerk's Ralf & Florian for his Quietus Baker's Dozen (2013), says its "fluid electronics" have "to a certain extent" influenced the flute playing of Tom Crossley, who plays with the band.
The reference work Contemporary Musicians names the Swell Maps and the Modern Lovers as the Pastels' two greatest influences.
Peter Momtchiloff of Talulah Gosh to Aesthetics for Birds (2014): "The basis of our music was the bringing-together of our two main influences, 1960s girl groups and the Ramones."

Amelia Fletcher of Talulah Gosh to The Quietus (2014): bands like the Pastels "twinned leather trousers with anoraks; it was that combination of seeing the world through a child's eye but also having a darker, harsher side which we wanted to get across."

Amelia Fletcher of Heavenly, interviewed by Quinn Moreland (2024), on touring Olympia and discovering Bratmobile and Bikini Kill: "we were inspired by the slightly more aggressive sound of riot grrrl, even though we never really sounded like a riot grrrl band."

Peter Momtchiloff of Heavenly to Aesthetics for Birds (2014), on touring the US in the early 1990s: "we met and played with Bratmobile and other riot grrrl acts, and found them kindred spirits. This reawakened our punk rock tendencies... and so our music became noisier from our 1993 releases till we finished in 1996."

Brian Nelson of Black Tambourine to Clash (2010): "The Jesus And Mary Chain were an enormous influence on us and they took a lot from the girl group, 60s sound... and we just wanted to do the same thing."

Brian Nelson of Black Tambourine to Clash (2010), on the band's formative years: "We always knew of American bands like Beat Happening, Galaxie 500, The Feelies – any of those bands were also hugely influential to us."

Brian Nelson of Black Tambourine to Clash (2010): "Galaxie 500, Yo La Tengo and things equally influenced us like that."

Mike Schulman of Black Tambourine to Ink 19 (2010): "For the noise stuff, I was especially interested in the NYC scene: Swans, Glenn Branca, Sonic Youth... I think our collective interest in noise was big factor in how BT sounded."

Lindsey Jordan said in a 2016 interview at the 9:30 Club, posted to Tumblr, that while writing Habit she was listening to a lot of Grouper, Broadcast, Joni Mitchell, Psychic TV, Beat Happening and Liz Phair, adding that not all of them influenced the album stylistically but she had learned from their songwriting.
Colin Newman of Wire to Pitchfork (2017): "In the period before I was living in London, I saw King Crimson more than any other band, and they had the biggest effect on me."

Nels Cline of Wilco, choosing Larks' Tongues in Aspic for Guitar Player's "10 records that changed my life" (2025): seeing the band as a teenager "made me want to write music that sounded like that, in my way."

Robert Pollard of Guided by Voices, choosing In the Court of the Crimson King for SPIN's "Records That Changed My Life" (2004): it led him into "a complete prog-rock phase", and "I've tried to write epics, but I've got a short attention span."
Bob Mould of Hüsker Dü, choosing Buzzcocks' Another Music in a Different Kitchen on Amoeba Music's What's In My Bag?: "Pete Shelley is like one of the main influences on my work."
A member of the Get Up Kids, on Amoeba Music's What's In My Bag?: "Fugazi is probably one of the most important bands for me personally, of how I found out about punk rock."

On Gang of Four's What's In My Bag? for Amoeba Music, with Jon King and Andy Gill, picking Bob Dylan's Don't Look Back: "The man who transformed my life when I first heard, you know, Highway 61 Revisited."
Mac DeMarco, picking the Modern Lovers on Amoeba Music's What's In My Bag?, of Jonathan Richman: "I love Jonathan. Huge inspiration for me."
A member of the Last Dinner Party, picking St. Vincent on Amoeba Music's What's In My Bag?: "I have a guitar, I play her guitar. My dad introduced her to me, probably when I was about, like, 14."

A member of Tortoise, picking a Tom Verlaine record on Amoeba Music's What's In My Bag?: "Television is sort of ground zero for me. I mean, they weren't my first favorite band, but they are my favorite band."

Simon Raymonde of Cocteau Twins, on Amoeba Music's What's In My Bag?, on seeing Patti Smith as a teenager: "She was just such an ethereal, beautiful soul. She became one of my heroines for many, many years."
Atsuo of Boris to Rad Company (c. 2005), on Akuma no Uta's sleeve copying Bryter Layter: "I love Nick Drake. I respect him... So people might understand Nick Drake's music has influenced our music."
Atsuo of Boris to Rad Company (c. 2005): "as a musician, I'm influenced by people like Nick Cave," and "I want to be Nick Cave as a drummer."
Atsuo of Boris to Rad Company (c. 2005), asked about his favourite drummers: "But aside from drummers, Iggy Pop, Ted Nugent, Nick Cave. Those people influenced me more than any drummers."

Wayne Coyne of the Flaming Lips, in his Quietus Baker's Dozen (2011), on putting on "a record like Boris or Yo La Tengo" on long drives, "big soundscapes that just dig into oblivion": "We've really embraced that in the past couple of years: to find this perfect goal, a sound you can play over and over... to get to the edge and stay there."

Chino Moreno of Deftones, choosing Hum's You'd Prefer an Astronaut for his Quietus Baker's Dozen (2010): "it's where Deftones get a big part of our influence from, tone-wise... a lot of that has directly inspired certain songs."
Chino Moreno of Deftones to Revolver (2011), on Loveless: making White Pony, "I played Loveless for Terry; I was like, 'I want to get the record to sound like this!'"
Chino Moreno of Deftones to Revolver (2011), on Pornography: "lyrically, that record has influenced me through a lot of the things that I've done."
Chino Moreno of Deftones to Rolling Stone (2015), on seeing Depeche Mode at his first concert: "I have a feeling it's what launched me into wanting to make music."
Chino Moreno of Deftones to NPR (2016): "my favorite band was like The Smiths or The Cure... so were basically just figuring it all out while we were also creating music."
Chino Moreno of Deftones to Revolver (2020), on early new wave "from OMD to Depeche Mode": "They've been a constant influence in pretty much all the music I've made throughout my life, I think."

Chino Moreno of Deftones to Revolver (2020), on first hearing the Human League's early records and the new wave around them: "They've been a constant influence in pretty much all the music I've made throughout my life, I think."
Chino Moreno of Deftones to Revolver (2020), asked which artists influenced White Pony's rock-meets-trip-hop sound: "DJ Shadow, of course, and even earlier stuff from the Nineties, like Portishead."

Chino Moreno of Deftones to Zane Lowe (2025), on watching the "Paranoid Android" video while writing Around the Fur: "just having my mind blown, like how music can be anything... when I watched them do that, I was like, 'You know, we could do anything.'"
Conor Curley of Fontaines D.C. to Guitar World (2024), on the guitars of Romance: "I was a lot more inspired by early 2000s, heavier rock music like Deftones."

Ben Weinman of the Dillinger Escape Plan to Machine Music (2021): the band set out to bring people "the feeling and experience that people were getting from the original hardcore bands like Bad Brains and Black Flag."

Ben Weinman of the Dillinger Escape Plan to Machine Music (2021): the band set out to bring people "the feeling and experience that people were getting from the original hardcore bands like Bad Brains and Black Flag."

Ben Weinman of the Dillinger Escape Plan to Mondo Sonoro (2019), asked how Mr. Bungle most influenced the band: "in our thirst for diversity and the irony in our music" (translated from the Spanish), adding that Mr. Bungle "were a great inspiration to us."
Ben Weinman of the Dillinger Escape Plan to Machine Music (2021), on Depeche Mode, the first band he was obsessed with as a teenager: "I'm sure melodically it inspired me and definitely culturally."

Ben Weinman of the Dillinger Escape Plan, choosing Fugazi's Repeater for The Skinny's "Under the Influence" (2013), his ten records that shaped his guitar playing: "Repeater was a record that was meant to be performed."

Ben Weinman of the Dillinger Escape Plan, choosing In the Court of the Crimson King for The Skinny's "Under the Influence" (2013), his ten records that shaped his guitar playing: "This band represented a time when music truly had no boundaries."

Jacob Bannon of Converge, choosing Disintegration for his Quietus Baker's Dozen (2026): "When I heard that record, it made me feel like it was okay to do that - where I could write from a personal perspective and not feel like the world was going to end."

Jacob Bannon of Converge to Westword (2011), asked whether Black Flag were an influence: "Oh definitely. Any early punk and hardcore, especially the work ethic... is something that's inspired by people like early Black Flag members."

Jacob Bannon of Converge, in Vice's Rank Your Records (2017), on the early band: Drive Like Jehu and the noise-rock bands he and Kurt Ballou "were starting to get into" set them apart, "and you almost hear that in the songs."

Wikipedia's Mike Patton page says that in 1992 he cited Nomeansno and the Residents as influences (Guitar Magazine), and that the members of Mr. Bungle often travelled to watch Nomeansno play live (Decibel).
Converge's Jacob Bannon and Nate Newton, picking NoMeansNo's Wrong on Amoeba Music's What's In My Bag?: "It's a huge, huge influence on both of us. This was a game-changing record for me."
Hugo Burnham of Gang of Four, picking Bowie's Ziggy Stardust on Amoeba Music's What's In My Bag?: "the record that changed my life, our lives... that just took us into a whole new world."
Kevin Parker of Tame Impala, picking Can's Future Days on Amoeba Music's What's In My Bag?: "These guys kind of taught me that band music can feel like electronic music."

A member of Interpol, picking Bad Brains' ROIR cassette on Amoeba Music's What's In My Bag?, on growing up near DC's hardcore scene: "I was kind of weaned on that... This is the record that really reeled me in."
A member of Interpol, picking Aphex Twin on Amoeba Music's What's In My Bag?: "I think he's one of the great songwriters, period. And he certainly had a big influence on me."

Michelle Zauner of Japanese Breakfast, picking Cat Power on Amoeba Music's What's In My Bag?: "I really love this album, and it inspires my writing a lot. Cat Power has always been a huge inspiration to me."

beabadoobee on Amoeba Music's What's In My Bag?, of Chino Moreno: "He's like my main inspiration of how I move on stage, especially with this new record"; in an earlier episode she recalls "being in Oxford with my band and just getting really into Deftones."

Kevin Parker of Tame Impala, picking White Pony on Amoeba Music's What's In My Bag?, on his teenage years: he "was obsessed with this album. I had been into a lot of nu metal and stuff from when I was a kid."

Brian Eno, choosing Reich's Early Works for his Quietus Baker's Dozen: hearing it, "my life changed"; its idea of loops running out of sync "became my go-to technique for making something interesting straight away."
Rhys Chatham, choosing Piano Phase for his Quietus Baker's Dozen: "That cascading phasing riff effect was directly inspired by Steve Reich's Piano Phase."
Ollie Judge of Squid, in the band's own notes on Bright Green Field for Apple Music, on "Documentary Filmmaker": "It was quite Steve Reich-inspired."

David Pajo of Slint, choosing Music for 18 Musicians for his Quietus Baker's Dozen: "I've spent decades trying to make music that recreates the uplifting feeling this record gives me... Reich was the only composer we were into back in the 80s."
Steve Holmes of American Football, in Vice's oral history of the band: "Freshman year, I was turned on to a lot of the bands that would influence our sound," Steve Reich among them.
Colin Newman of Wire, choosing Music for 18 Musicians for his Quietus Baker's Dozen, on hearing Piano Phase on his first day at art school: "It completely blew my mind."
Bradford Cox of Deerhunter to Pitchfork, choosing Reich's Drumming for the year he turned 20: "I was searching for this minimalist mindset where you could be calm and tranced out."

Jarvis Cocker to Pitchfork, on 1978, the year Pulp formed: seeing Devo play Sheffield City Hall "was quite influential. One of the first songs that Pulp learned how to play was the Devo song 'Gut Feeling.'"
A. Savage of Parquet Courts, on "Total Football" in NPR's track-by-track of Wide Awake!: "The bass line of the song was inspired by Devo."
Stu Mackenzie of King Gizzard to Loudwire: "Kraftwerk and Devo, that type of thing definitely has influenced Gizz a lot over the years."

Robert Pollard of Guided by Voices, choosing Devo's debut for SPIN's "Records That Changed My Life" (2004): "it just blew my mind how good it was. To me, it was progressive rock because it was taking music in a new direction."
Kurt Cobain, asked in a 1993 Rio de Janeiro interview to name bands that influenced him, as quoted by Far Out: "The B-52's, Devo, you know, anything... Ramones."

Doug McCombs of Tortoise, choosing Devo's Duty Now for the Future for his Quietus Baker's Dozen, on hearing it as a teenager: "I have no idea what appealed to me about it other than the sheer strangeness. Duty Now was the second record I owned."
Mark Mothersbaugh of Devo, on Eno's synth solo in Roxy Music's "Editions of You": "it totally helped me turn my world upside down to find a direction to how to look for sound and how to experiment."
Dan Snaith of Caribou, choosing World of Echo for his Quietus Baker's Dozen, on singing on his own records: "people like Arthur Russell are the reason that I figured out how to make it work."
Dev Hynes of Blood Orange, choosing Russell's Calling Out of Context for his Quietus Baker's Dozen: "it's an understatement to say it changed my music and my life in general."
Tyler Hyde of Black Country, New Road, choosing Russell's Love Is Overtaking Me for her Quietus Baker's Dozen: "I have embarrassingly tried to use his influence with my lyrics in the past."

rejectedEdges.citation: John Lydon, in Pitchfork's 5-10-15-20: "I had little time for what was coming out of America; bands like Television never really grabbed me, I just couldn't connect."
Colin Newman of Wire, in Pitchfork's 5-10-15-20, on 1979: "We studiously ignored Joy Division because they seemed a little too derivative of us."

Michael Gira, interviewed by The Wire (republished by Young God Records), on playing under Glenn Branca: it was an inspiration, "But Branca was NOT a musical influence, more an ideal of what it's possible to achieve through sound."
The Guardian (18 Aug 2020): Elizabeth Fraser "was often cited as an influence on Birgisson at the start of his career, only he'd never heard a note of her music."
Angel Olsen to Time Out Istanbul, asked about songwriters from Patti Smith to PJ Harvey: "I didn't grow up listening to any of those ladies."
Clash reports that PJ Harvey says she hadn't heard of Patti Smith until critics started comparing them.

Ian MacKaye to Gothamist: "I remember in the beginning of Fugazi everyone was saying 'Oh clearly these guys have listened to a lot of Gang of Four.' But I had never listened to Gang of Four so it wasn't actually accurate." He adds that the songs being compared were his own, written before Guy Picciotto began contributing: "Guy was a fan of Gang of Four but the stuff people were comparing to Gang of Four was written by me before Guy started contributing compositions." Logged contested rather than clean precisely because MacKaye confirms Picciotto's fandom -- the denial covers the songs at issue and MacKaye's own listening, not every member.
Paul Banks/Interpol guitarist Daniel Kessler has denied the comparison across 2002, 2007 and 2012 interviews: "It has absolutely nothing to do with me. I don't know where that shit comes from."
The only documented connection is that Steve Shelley drummed on Cat Power's first two albums -- personnel, not a stated influence.
Tom Verlaine resisted the comparison across numerous interviews, naming Albert Ayler and John Coltrane as his real touchstones instead.
Nick Zinner has rejected the comparison; the only positive evidence found for it was an editorially-curated Apple Music playlist, not an artist statement.

Natalie Mering has said she has always liked Nico but could never fully relate to her, unable to relate to her life and feeling Nico had the advantage of being extremely beautiful -- admiration paired with an explicit reservation.
Producer Brad Wood has said Liz Phair's chord shapes "have more to do with like, Glenn Branca than Joni Mitchell" -- an insider contradicting a comparison Phair herself hasn't addressed.
Mark E. Smith called David Bowie "crap," grouping him with Genesis, Pink Floyd and James Taylor.
MOJO reported that Mark E. Smith visibly shivers at the comparison to Bob Dylan.
Tommy Ramone's Rock and Roll Hall of Fame induction remarks explicitly separated the band's CBGB-era peers, including Television, from the artists who actually influenced them.
The same Rock and Roll Hall of Fame remarks in which Tommy Ramone separated Television from the band's influences apply equally to Talking Heads, another CBGB-era peer rather than a stated influence.

Far Out Magazine, asked whether Swans' live cover of "Love Will Tear Us Apart" was a tribute to Ian Curtis, Michael Gira dispelled the argument that he is in any way indebted to the Joy Division frontman.

Louder Than War (2014), Andrew Savage by email: says Pavement isn't a big influence and that Parquet Courts share similar influences instead, naming the Velvet Underground, Roxy Music and the Fall. Malkmus's remark about mistaking a Parquet Courts song for his own band is a third-party comparison; Savage's response in Hot Press is bemusement.

NOW Magazine (2016), Will Toledo asked directly: he grew up on the Beatles, the Who, the Kinks and the Beach Boys, explicitly not Pavement, Sonic Youth or Dinosaur Jr, attributing the resemblance to those bands having listened to the same older music he did.
Same NOW Magazine (2016) quote as the Pavement denial -- Toledo names the Beatles, the Who, the Kinks and the Beach Boys as his actual upbringing, explicitly not Sonic Youth.
Same NOW Magazine (2016) quote as the Pavement denial -- Toledo names the Beatles, the Who, the Kinks and the Beach Boys as his actual upbringing, explicitly not Dinosaur Jr.
Westword: a "pet peeve" Toledo says he's heard since 2011; he never really listened to the Strokes -- a commonality of influence, not descent.

INDY Week interview: the interviewer proposes Prefab Sprout, Thomas Dolby and Gary Numan as reference points for ken; Dan Bejar redirects to something more basic -- New Order, the Cure, Echo & the Bunnymen. The Numan framing came from the interviewer's question, not Bejar's answer.

Westword (2010), asked about Tori Amos/Kate Bush comparisons: Annie Clark says she loves Kate Bush but doesn't feel she's carrying on her tradition, and was "probably more influenced by Stravinsky" on that record -- then discusses "Wuthering Heights" admiringly and technically (the harmony, the bar of fifths in the chorus) as a valuable lesson. Georgia Straight's fourteen-year retrospective does list Kate Bush among her invaluable influences. Admiration and technical study alongside an explicit refusal of the lineage framing. Recorded for its own sake -- kate-bush isn't a graph node.
Matt Berninger's much-quoted line: the Strokes influenced more bands in ten years than the artists he named did in twenty-five -- a claim about their importance, not his own descent.

Berninger calls Arcade Fire "hugely influential to aspiring musicians" with a direct connection to people's hearts -- a compliment about their reach, not a stated influence on The National; also chronologically awkward.

Westword: asked whether the Chameleons, Comsat Angels and the Sound informed Interpol's sound alongside Joy Division, Paul Banks said he'd never heard any of those bands before starting Interpol, and has only heard the Chameleons since the band put out records.

Louder Than War: Mark Burgess says he saw Joy Division live five or six times and found them "a bit of a mess early on" without feeling musically influenced by them, though he took notice once Closer came out, calling it "on a different level."
Rolling Stone, "The Cranberries: The Hidden Power of Dreams": Noel Hogan says "If we do sound like other bands, like the Sundays, then that's coincidence."

Labrador Records interview: Johan Duncanson, asked about the constant My Bloody Valentine/Jesus and Mary Chain comparisons, dismissed the latter directly -- "jamc is a boring and very heterosexual rock band that wrote a few good songs" -- while affirming a genuine appreciation for My Bloody Valentine in the same breath.

A Fall 2006 Q&A archived at content.jasonmolina.org: asked about Leonard Cohen comparisons, Jason Molina said he "didn't hear a single song I know of by Leonard Cohen until I was about out of college, so it would be hard to call him a regular influence."

Victoria Legrand to Drowned In Sound (Nov 2007): "I personally don't hear the ostentatious similarity with our music and the Cocteau Twins." Alex Scally, separately: "We didn't really listen to them. Strangely, they weren't part of us." Contested rather than clean because an unverified later report has Legrand professing admiration for the band -- but a favourites statement is a weaker claim than a shaping influence two members explicitly reject.

Kurt Cobain to Jon Savage (New York, 22 July 1993), asked directly about his influences: "I stayed away from Joy Division. I've heard a few of their songs and I know I would really like it, but just the mystique about it and the stories I've heard, I know that's the band to listen to, of all of them. I'm just waiting." The handwritten top-50 album list in his Journals carries no Joy Division entry either.

Gary Numan on Amoeba Music's What's In My Bag?: "A lot of people think I was influenced by Kraftwerk. I wasn't, actually, other than it was electronic," adding that it "was no influence at all, just wasn't what I wanted to do." In 1979 he had credited them.

Isaac Brock to The Rocket (summer 1997): "I'm scared to death of becoming a band like Pavement" -- they "put out a really amazing album, Slanted and Enchanted, that had a really great feeling, and somewhere they lost it. They got overproduced." Contested rather than clean because he praises the record in the same breath; what he rejects is Pavement as a model, not their existence in his listening.
